speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
that Bill C-26, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pride that I rise to speak on second reading of Bill C-26, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act. This Bill will always have special significance for me in that it is the first piece of social policy legislation that I, as Minister of National Health and Welfare representing the Government of Canada, have the opportunity to present to the House. This Bill will correct a very serious social problem which has long concerned myself and almost all Members of the House of Commons.
The Bill before us today will extend the protection of the spouse's allowance program to all widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64 regardless of the age of their spouse at death. This proposal was a firm commitment made to the people of Canada during the last election campaign. It was formally enunciated in the Speech from the Throne in November. I am pleased that the Government of Canada is fulfilling another of its election promises this morning.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The group I am referring to today represents approximately 85,000 Canadians who are widowed and between the eligible ages which I have already announced. It is important to note as well that the vast majority, an estimated 72,000 of the 85,000 who are eligible, are widowed women. I do not think there is a more important cause to which the House of Commons can address itself than the financial situation which these people are now in. This legislation does not and cannot consider the separation, sense of loss or loneliness which these people experience. Those highly personal conditions can be addressed only by individuals interacting with those people. I believe that, within the economic restraints of the country, it is incumbent on us as legislators to address the economic realities these people face.
Since coming into office the Government has had to face up to the very sad fact that the state of finances of the Government of Canada were in even worse shape than we had been led to believe. As the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) has told Canadians, tough measures will be required to reduce a deficit which has been allowed to skyrocket over the past decade.
However, we cannot and will not allow a very vulnerable segment of Canada's near elderly population to continue to suffer because of circumstances completely beyond their control. There is an urgent need which has been consistently identified by present and past Members of the House of Commons as well as other members of society. Low-income widowed persons aged 60 to 64 do not have many of the options available to most of us. For instance, the vast majority of the persons who will benefit from this Bill are women who have been financial dependants for most, if not all, of their lives. They did not question this financial dependence because society deemed it appropriate. Societal norms dictated that the husband would enter the labour force and earn the money while the wife stayed in the home and performed the unpaid role of mother, housekeeper, companion, nurse, guidance counsellor and community worker-the list is endless. If the wife did take a job it was most often as a secondary earner to supplement the family budget.
I believe that the Bill before us today recognizes that contribution in part. I know that one cannot quantify that contribution in financial terms. So often in our society we want to put a financial value on service or work. No matter what Members may feel about the Bill with regard to whether it goes far enough, I think they would agree that the contribution these people have made to our society goes beyond financial measure. All of us realize that today is but a small recognition of the contribution that they have made to each one of us.
While there will be men who benefit from this proposal, there is no denying that poverty is largely a woman's problem and that widows in particular are among the poorest. These women have held down numerous responsible jobs throughout their adult lives and are more experienced and capable than many people are after spending 40 years in the paid labour force.
Let's not kid ourselves: in most instances, the 60 to 64-year old widow is not the one the personnel manager will hire. Why hire someone who might have only a few years until retirement while there are other young and perhaps better educated people competing for job openings available today? Therefore society must show compassion for these near elderly widows.

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act
Compassion is what Bill C-26 is all about. Widowed persons aged 60 to 64, effective September of this year, will be guaranteed a level of income with which to meet their basic living costs. They will not be well off by any means, but they will no longer be destitute.
I believe that the best way of explaining this proposal is first to look at the evolution of income-tested assistance for persons in the 60 to 64-year age group. In 1973 the federal and provincial Governments undertook a complete review of Canada's social security system. During this review various options for a program of income support and supplementation for all low-income Canadians was studied. The federal Government advanced a proposal to the provinces in early 1976, but due to a lack of clear response on the part of the provinces, the proposal was withdrawn in 1977.
In the meantime the federal Government had already introduced the income support concept for elderly couples by means of a spouse's allowance program. Under this program which began in 1975, an income-tested benefit became payable to the 60 to 64-year old spouse of a low-income old age security pensioner. This step was taken in recognition of the fact that many of these elderly couples had no income apart from one basic old age security pension and a single guaranteed income supplement. That was little enough for one person to live on and far too little for two.
Since the beginning of the spouse's allowance program, there has been continuous pressure for the federal Government to expand this benefit to include other needy persons in the near elderly category. To date there have been two extensions to the spouse's allowance program. Originally, the spouse's allowance ceased to be paid when the pensioner spouse had died. In 1978 the federal Government introduced a Bill which resulted in the allowance being paid for six months following the pensioner's death. The theory was that this would give the widowed spouse time to adjust to a changed situation before losing the benefit, but it really just prolonged the agony of a situation that was often inescapable. In truth, there was no good reason why 60 to 64-year old widows and widowers who had been relying on the spouse's allowance program to make ends meet should lose their allowances until they became eligible for the old age security pension at age 65.
For this reason, when the Progressive Conservative Government came to power in 1979 we further amended the spouse's allowance program. As a result of that legislation, a widowed spouse's allowance recipient in need can continue to receive the allowance until age 65. I am proud today, on behalf of the Government, to extend that commitment that we made in opposition and that step we took in government in 1979. Those objectives and commitments for those less fortunate than most Canadians are again being extended further today.
During the debate on the amendment, Members of the Government were the first to admit that many more elderly persons in need were still excluded from the spouse's allowance program. Nevertheless, we did not feel we could go further
until such time as an extensive review of Canada's retirement income system was concluded. Such a review was conducted in 1983, by a special Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform which released its findings in December of that year. Among the Task Force's many proposals was the extension of spouse's allowance to all low-income widowed persons 60 to 64 years of age. I am pleased that the Task Force on Pension Reform made that proposal, and I am pleased that this Government is coming forward in a legislative forum to give life to that proposal.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I would be remiss at this point if I did not give recognition to Members in this House who are members of that Task Force. The Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) was the Chairman of that Task Force, and as Chairman he signed the report. I commend him for his foresight.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

There are other members of the Task Force whom I cannot name at this time, but I know they represent members from all political parties and I thank them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
There is one aspect of this legislation, possibly two, that Members will want to identify as not going far enough. First is the matter of whether this Bill could extend the same benefits to Canadians who are separated, divorced and single. I do not have the ability to take each
February 4, 1985

individual case of people who would fall into those categories and say that they are not as much in need as the group to which this legislation addresses itself. I think Members would recognize that the most urgent as a group-and I am not arguing individual cases could not be raised to make the other point-to which this legislation addresses itself are those in greatest need.
The other point I raised for the consideration of the House is whether legislation of this type, with a Charter coming into effect on April 17, and other social policy legislation could be challenged under the terms of the Charter. When you look at our social policy legislation, Mr. Speaker, you will note obviously that it discerns on the basis of age. Those 65 and over get an old age pension and those who are younger do not. It discerns on the basis of people who are eligible for family allowance; for example, if they have dependent children. An argument might be put forward that the legislation discriminates on the basis of marital status.
If I could speak personally for a moment, I had some involvement with the discussions on the Constitution and the Charter of Rights. No matter what viewpoints were put forward, either for or against the Charter, when the discussions were completed I do not believe any Member of the House wanted the Charter to be interpreted in such a manner that legislation such as we have before us today, and principles upon which social policy legislation is founded, could be brought into question or jeopardized.
While some might want to raise it as a point of discussion, I suggest that if that argument is taken to its most logical conclusion, the only manner in which one could address social policy and benefits would possibly be by providing a guaranteed annual income for everyone. While I am not deprecating that viewpoint, I place that caution before the House. Before that position is taken too strongly, proponents of that view should look very seriously not only at present legislation but at collective agreements, for example, and how they could be affected.
I should like to make one further point; it is the real reason this legislation appeals to me. In the years I have had the honour to represent my constituency in the House since 1972-I think both Members who came into the House in this Parliament and those who have been here a longer period of time would agree-without question the most difficult cases with which I have had to deal were those of women who made the contribution of which we have spoken as mother, spouse and so forth. They had made that contribution but were unable to contribute to a pension plan because they were "not earning a regular income". They had lost their spouse and if he was a person of pensionable age, that pension was gone. Not only had they suffered a personal loss, they had limited financial resources. We went through the various steps of what the pension might be for which they might be eligible and came down to one quiet statement-and I am sure all of us have made it; "Well, Madam, there is always social assist-
Old Age Security Act
ance". That is not good enough for the contribution these women have made to Canada. It is not good enough to tell individuals that the best we can do for them is welfare.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
As I said, this proposal will extend important financial assistance to an estimated 85,000 widowed persons. These are low-income Canadians. I have already given the estimates of the number of people involved in terms of male and female. These widowed persons will be guaranteed the same minimum income as that already being provided to other widowed spousal allowance recipients. The monthly benefit, which is $536.26 currently and which will be somewhat higher by September due to quarterly cost of living increases, certainly will not put these low-income 62-to 64-year olds on Easy Street. Nevertheless, it will give them an income which is enough to live on and place them in a better situation than they are now. It is something many have gone without for much too long.
This proposal is not inexpensive. To provide this very necessary financial assistance will cost approximately $190 million in fiscal 1985-86 beginning in September, while in the first full year of implementation, 1985-87, the cost will be $350 million. As I have said, the cost is high, but I am sure Hon. Members will agree it is an expense that the country must afford.
Just to elaborate the point a little further for those who say the Bill does not go far enough, the cost estimate of including everyone is in the order of $1.5 billion. When we look at the financial resources of the country, there are two questions to answer. The first is, if we cannot include everyone, should we not do anything? The other question is whether we do what we can for those in greatest need. Obviously that is the approach we have taken. While this Bill proposes that the extended spouse's allowance benefit become effective in September, 1985, it is very important that this legislation be passed now. Given prompt passage, we will have ample time for potential beneficiaries to apply, for the advertising campaign, so that they can become eligible by September, 1985. I do not have to remind Hon. Members, I am sure, that a fair amount of personal paperwork as well as governmental organization has to take place before the program can be implemented.
There are 85,000 Canadians that this Government has to contact, 85,000 applications that have to be completed and sent in and 85,000 new payment files that have to be prepared. On top of this, it is imperative that we co-operate with the provinces to ensure that where a provincial program is affected by this SPA program, the transition be made as smoothly as possible.
This Government is the first to acknowledge that there are other near-elderly persons in need who remain excluded from the important financial protection provided by the spouse's allowance program. However, as was recognized by the all party Task Force, the Government of Canada, in other words the Canadian people, cannot at this time go much beyond the

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act
proposals we have made. What we can do and must do, given current economic circumstances, is to take this next logical step in extending the spouse's allowance program. The other most logical step after this legislation is seriously to take the pension reform proposals that have been made both by the task force and by other groups and give them life over the course of the mandate of this Government. That is the commitment that we have made. As Members will note, this is but one element of a commitment to a goal we have as a government.
In conclusion, I am filled with great gratitude, which I extend both to my Cabinet colleagues and my colleagues in the House. No matter what is said of Parliament and its lack of response, to me, on this issue they have all responded and I thank them for it.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, before getting into the main elements of my speech today I want to indicate-this may come as a surprise to some of the political novices in this House-that there are times in the life of a Parliament in which all Members of the House will congratulate and applaud a decision by the Government. The announcement today by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) is the kind that will receive the acceptance of Members of all Parties in this House.
With regard to the goodwill and importance of this legislation today, I congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I also congratulate the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). Over the years she has spent a great deal of time promoting the cause of the extension of such legislation to include largely the women in our society but also others who have been left out from some of the social legislation which has been introduced in the House over the years.
While I am in the congratulatory phase of my remarks, the one person I think should be recognized is not here today but usually sits at the table of the Officers in the afternoons. I am speaking of Stanley Knowles, the former Member of Parliament for Winnipeg North Centre.
Hear, hear!

I recognize his personal contributions. It has been a lifetime quest of his to improve benefits to the elderly in our society. Had he still been sitting here as a Member of Parliament, I am sure he above all would applaud the decision made by the Government today to extend the spousal allowance to ail those between the ages of 60 and 64 who are widows or widowers.
I do not wish to make the congratulatory phase of my remarks too long. I noted that the Minister of National Health and Welfare was rather non-partisan in his remarks except on a couple of occasions. He was mildly partisan on those occasions and I will say that my two interventions in that sense will be mild as well.
The Minister mentioned earlier in his discussion that part of the problem of not being able to extend the measures beyond those put forward today was caused by the economic situation in which the Government found itself when it took office. However, I would like to remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare that above and beyond his duties as a Minister of the Crown, one of the prime responsibilities of a Minister of Health and Welfare within the Cabinet system is to be a protector of the poor and those with modest incomes.
I congratulate the Minister on being able to win round one of the battle by getting the $190 million required to extend this program today. I would also indicate that past Ministers of Health and Welfare have also been faced with the same economic difficulties in the large context. I point to the record of Monique Begin, a former Minister of National Health and Welfare who in 1980 increased the guaranteed income supplement by some $35 a month and, in the last year of our mandate, found the money, despite the economic difficulties and the size of the deficit, to increase the guaranteed income supplement by some $50 per month in the year 1984.
To a large extent this is an issue that extends beyond the bounds of politics. Therefore, I would like to indicate that many of the sentiments expressed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare are probably shared by most of the people in this room. Very early on he mentioned that of the 85,000 people who will be affected by today's decision, some 72,000 are women. In percentage terms that means that some 87.5 per cent of the recipients of today's announcement are women. This indicates that the problem about which to a great extent we learned through our work on the pensions task force is that we have almost institutionalized poverty among women in the country. This is not just a product of the inadequate system but a product of a society that has never really moved to address the issues of divorce reform, employment opportunities for women as compared to those for men and the discrepancy that exists between the pay levels for women and men in our society. A number of factors affect the final lifestyle of women in our society as they reach their retirement years.
At the outset, I would like to indicate that we as well would like to see some improvements made to the legislation that is being tabled today. I noticed that the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated that part of the problem with this legislation concerns whether or not it contravenes the Charter or Rights. The indications that I have from a legal perspective is that it would not. It may in fact contradict the human rights code because we are not supposed to discriminate on the basis of marital status. A decision would have to be made by the courts to determine whether or not this is a good or a bad service. That is part of the problem, from a government standpoint, of trying to extend this provision to cover others in our society between the ages of 60 and 64 who are divorced or single. Members of any caucus will eloquently plead the case that the Government should extend the guaranteed income supplement to those individuals as well.
The Minister briefly touched upon the other problem that exists. He indicated that there are some 85,000 new recipients
February 4, 1985

of this benefit and this will require the Filling in of a great many forms. There is bureaucratic process that must be undergone in order to put these people on the guaranteed income supplement scheme. If possible, I could speak to the Opposition House Leader and indicate to him that quick passage in committee could speed up the process so that we may be able to have this measure instituted by June rather than September.
Hear, hear!

In addition, I want to talk a bit about the reason why we have allowed our society to evolve to the extent that we find that 87 per cent of the people who will qualify for this measure are women. Members of all three political Parties have advocated very eloquently the necessity for improvements in various pieces of legislation so that the next generation of Canadians will not find itself in the same situation in which this generation has found itself of having in fact institutionalized poverty among women in our society.
We spoke a bit about the requirement for pension reform. I know the Minister of Employment and Immigration and I were probably the first to promote within our own committee the extension of the Canada Pension Plan to include homemakers. I know as well as I know that I am standing here that pension reform is high on the list of reforms planned by the Government. The situation would have been the same if the Liberal Party had been in power. In fact, there are periods in our history in which a particular goal may be achieved. I believe that pension reform is here. It is my understanding that there has been a consensus package agreed to for reform in the private pension plan systems. With some small amount of negotiation, I believe a package could be ready to be put forward to all the provincial Governments in the next 12 months. I think that would go a long way toward removing for the next generation of men and women alike the spectre of poverty in their elderly years.
I now return to the homemakers' pension proposal. I know that the Minister of Employment and Immigration and I spoke a bit about this but were never able to convince the majority of the committee members to undertake this kind of reform. In light of announcements made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in the last two weeks, there may well be the possibility of allowing members of the Cabinet within the Cabinet structure to promote that idea. I hope they will listen as I outline it to them.
There is a need for pension reform. There is a problem with pension coverage. However, I must admit that today's generation of Canadians, women and men alike, are not facing the same demographics that were faced by our parents' generation. As a result, with some adequate improvements in the Federal Standards Benefits Act and in April's Budget, I think we can begin taking steps toward improving the situation for the Canadians of today's working generation.
The way the pension legislation exists today, one must be age 45 or have worked for ten years for the same company in order to receive both one's own pension contributions and the
Old Age Security Act
contributions of one's employer. Very early on we recognized there are two emerging trends that indicate that the existing pension legislation is not adequate. First, the emerging work pattern indicates that many more Canadians of this generation can be expected to be more mobile in their quest for employment and perhaps may work in two or three different provinces. More than likely they are going to have to undertake periods of retraining in their lifetimes. Today's fast-emerging technological changes in the workplace indicate that workers will probably require some retraining in their lifetimes. This means that work sharing or part-time work will be more prevalent than it has been in the past.
Workers will have to be more mobile in their quest for employment and therefore it is imperative that we change the pension legislation to reflect that reality. There should be an earlier locking in of the employer and employee contributions and the system should be made more portable. Part-time workers should be covered in the same way full-time workers are by pensions. Pieces of legislation must be changed federally as well as provincially. I hope all of us are cognizant of the need for speed in the passage of these kinds of improvements to our legislation.
The issue of part-time work is a women's issue as well. Far more women than men find themselves being part-time workers or shared workers. To a large extent, the issues of improved survivors' benefits and divorce reform are women's issues as well. Under the existing laws, today's pension assets are not divisible upon marriage breakdown. I do not particularly like the emerging family pattern which is evolving, but as legislators we must realize that the divorce rate is affecting 50 per cent of the population. The laws must reflect the emerging family pattern. As well, the laws must reflect the emerging work pattern. Other critics from my caucus will be indicating their desired improvements in the legislation, particularly with respect to women's issues.
I want to return to the subject of homemakers; I know it is at the heart of the negotiations between the federal Government and the Provinces. As we are aware, it requires the approval of two-thirds of the provinces, representing two-thirds of the population, to effect changes to the Canada Pension Plan. In effect, the Province of Ontario, because of its size and population, has the power of veto. I assume that the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Finance will be involved in the negotiations for the inclusion of homemakers in the Canada Pension Plan. I want to reiterate the importance of allowing that inclusion. I want to stress the importance of including homemakers in the pension plan, in the hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Employment and Immigration will take my arguments before Cabinet and convince their colleagues of the intelligence of my contributions.
There is a very poor understanding of the way in which the public pension system operates in Canada as opposed to the private pension system. It is at the heart of the political debate

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act
and it will be at the heart of the ability of political parties to generate the political will to undertake the necessary reforms which must be made to the pension system. Many people are worried that when they retire in 2004 there will not be a viable Canada Pension Plan which will allow them to have an adequate pension.
I want to go back almost 20 years, to 1966, to indicate to the House why the existing pension plan evolved to the state it is at today and the improvements which can be made to it. In 1966 there were 14 workers for every person over the age of 65. Had we allowed the public pension plan to be funded the same way as a private plan, there would have been a rapid increase in the surplus of the fund, to the extent that the Government could have purchased 58 per cent of the Toronto Stock Exchange. There was concern in 1966 about the magnitude of the surplus which was being held in the hands of the Government. Therefore, the funding mechanisms for the public pension plan were devised in a manner totally different from the private pension plan. In essence, a "pay-go" system was allowed. In other words, enough money was collected each year to pay the pension requirements and to have a two to three-year surplus. That was the essence of the funding mechanism for the Canada Pension Plan. Basically, the plan considered only men in 1966. That is why homemakers were not included.
In 1966 our fathers did not have access to private pension plans and were facing retirement without adequate pension assets. In their lifetimes they paid taxes which built up the infrastructure for universities, roads and hospitals. Therefore, we transferred the burden from one generation to another. In 1966 the young workers in Canada indicated that they would supply their fathers with an adequate pension in order that they could live their twilight years in relative comfort. The younger generation accepted the burden of paying for that pension. Everyone who has collected a pension in the last 20 years has paid only 17 cents of every dollar which was taken. The remaining 83 cents was paid for by the next generation. No one quarrelled with the transfer of that burden. However, in 1966 women were not included. Why did we not include our mothers? They worked just as hard to build a family life and they allowed Canadian society to expand. Therefore, I would plead, along with the Minister of Employment and Immigration, that homemakers should be included in the revisions which will be made to the Canada Pension Plan.
If we are going to change the contribution rates to the Canada Pension Plan, there should be a debate on the floor of the House of Commons to improve the plan beyond the inclusion of homemakers. Two weeks ago the Minister of Finance met with his provincial counterparts in Montreal. At that meeting it was agreed that the contribution rates to the Canada Pension Plan would be increased significantly. The definition of "significant" will determine the extent to which the surplus beyond our expectations will develop within the Canada Pension Plan. The Minister of Employment and Immigration will remember the debate in which the Liberal Party recommended that the "pay-go" philosophy should not
be altered significantly. As I indicated earlier, the "pay-go" system meant that the money which was collected in one year was adequate to meet the pay-out level of the fund, with a possible cushion of a two to three-year surplus.
Those were the demographics which we witnessed when we made the recommendations some 18 months ago. It meant that significant increases were not required to the pension plan premiums. It required some increases, but the increases could have been phased in very gradually to the point at which, to have it fully paid by the year 2030, it would require approximately 10 per cent of the average take-home pay to cover the costs. If the decision of the provinces is to go beyond the "pay-go" system-and that is the heart of the matter which is before Cabinet-with a two to three-year cushion, and if the decision will mean significant, front-ended increases, it will result in a massive build up of surplus funds.
In our Task Force report on the Canada Pension Plan, we indicated that if the decision was made to go beyond the "pay-go" system, then three questions had to be asked. First, what will be the size of the surplus? Second, who will control the funds? Third, to what use will those funds be put? We indicated that those questions had to be addressed if the Government ever changed the "pay-go" philosophy of the public pension plan system. I realize it is theoretical, but if the decision is made to go beyond the "pay-go" system in order to build up a surplus, then I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare might want to advocate other changes to the plan.
I agreed with the Minister when he mentioned earlier that in our political day-to-day life the major problem which we face is that of individuals who are between the ages of 55 and 64 who, through the death of their spouse, divorce or breakdown in the family pattern, Find themselves impoverished. The other area in which we face significant problems is that of an individual, male or female, who is the primary breadwinner in the family and who Finds himself or herself disabled through no fault of their own and has no access to long-term disability beneFits in the workplace. That person must rely solely on Canada Pension Plan disability payments.
I believe all of us recognize that that is an area which is woefully under-funded. In terms of improvements to the pension plan, I do not think any of us would stand in the way of improving the payments to disabled persons. I recommend that that cause should be advocated with respect to the increased surplus in the Canada Pension Plan.
I agree whole-heartedly with the inclusion of homemakers in the plan. That would go a long way to removing the stigma of poverty among today's elderly. I spoke earlier about the intergenerational transfer. In 1966 we told our fathers that we would give them a reasonable standard of living in their retirement years and, because we had jobs, we told them that we would accept the burden of paying for their pension. However, the problem today is of a different magnitude. The greatest problem which faces all political parties today is that of unemployment. Largely, but not exclusively, we have a youth unemployment rate which is significantly higher than
February 4, 1985

the national unemployment average. I am not trying to take away from those individuals who are middle-aged and find themselves unemployed, but specifically, I want to talk about youth unemployment.
In 1966 our youth transferred a gift to their parents. That gift was a retirement with reasonable expectations. If we talk to the people of Canada between the ages of 60 and 65 years who have paid off their mortgages, we find that they would like to have an early retirement but cannot do so because the Canada Pension Plan kicks in at age 65. There are also those who would like to have an actuarially-reduced Canada Pension Plan.
Perhaps the solution would be to transfer from that generation to the young generation the availability of a job and then they would receive the benefit of early retirement. I note that the Province of Quebec, which is the first province to go out of synchronization with the other provinces under the Quebec Pension Plan, allowed for the first time in history an actuarially-reduced Quebec Pension Plan. Some 50,000 Quebecers then decided to take early retirement. I do not know if there is a direct correlation between that and the unemployment rate in the Province of Quebec which has dropped from a year ago, but these are statistics which one might want to study.
Certainly, I would say that a beneficial use of those surplus funds, rather than giving them back out to the provinces at lower than prime rates, and a better use of those social funds, would be to address the number one problem in the country today, namely the unemployment problem. I say that not with any great knowledge of the statistics which would be required, but I know the Minister of Employment and Immigration, the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands, well remembers Mr. Michael Wolfson, and another person who has earned a great deal of our respect for his contribution to the pension task force and who now works for the Minister of National Health and Welfare, Mr. Michael Hatfield. It seems to me that one might want to be able to use some of those statistics in order to determine perhaps a better use of those surplus funds than others might envisage around the Cabinet table as those discussions take place.
Let me end, Mr. Speaker, by reiterating my congratulatory message at the beginning of my remarks to the Government for having brought in this particular piece of legislation. I cannot disagree with it. It reflects the recommendation which, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated, was one of the prime recommendations our Party made through our own pension task force.
Second, I would hope that in committee one might want to explore the possibility of improvements to the legislation by perhaps speeding up the process for a June delivery date rather than September.
Third-I know that others in my Party will want to promote this-would be the extension of the plan for people between the ages of 60 and 64 years on the basis only of income and not
Old Age Security Act
marital status. I know as sure as I am standing here that the Minister of National Health and Welfare fought hard for that.
I recognize that there are saw-offs around any Cabinet table when it comes to the distribution of dollars. I recognize the problem the Minister faces with the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), the Hon. Member for Yukon, and the Minister of Finance, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre, and I wish him well in trying to convince his Cabinet colleagues. I know some of his colleagues around the table probably think the same way he and I do and I would hope that he could convince the other neanderthal members of the Cabinet to see the progressive necessity of such a measure.
Finally, I want to say that I hope that in this particular session of Parliament we will see legislation which would allow the federal Government to become the most progressive in terms of Governments in our country which recognizes the need for pension reform, which recognizes that the issues of unemployment, pension reform and tax reform are very interrelated and, to a large extent, are women's problems. I hope that progress will be made in these areas, Mr. Speaker, and if progress can be made, let us hope it is accomplished with swift passage.

Mr. Speaker, I also wish to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) for bringing forward this measure to expand the application of the spouse's allowance. He should be especially congratulated, Mr. Speaker, because he chose this as the first piece of legislation to introduce into the House for debate. I am quite sure that the passage of this particular measure is guaranteed by all sides of the House.
Having made those complimentary remarks-I see the Minister is smiling; he did say earlier that he did not introduce this Bill without anticipating some negative comments and that perhaps he would be criticized for not taking the measure far enough-I want to assure the Minister that his predictions are absolutely right on. I intend to make a few comments about what I think are serious omissions in the measure brought forward by the Minister, although, as I have already indicated, this Bill will have the full support of myself and my caucus. We will do nothing at all to prevent its speedy passage.
I am, perhaps, at the point of making the Minister an offer which he cannot refuse. One aspect of the Bill, obviously, with which we are disappointed is the length of time it will take to put this measure in place. I believe there will be a ten-month delay until September. If it will accommodate the Minister in terms of bringing such a measure in by the end of this month, my Party would agree that I would be the only speaker. We could then get it through all stages as quickly as possible, if that would accommodate the Minister. If the Minister would agree to that, all he has to do is to send me a note and we will look upon it as kindly as possible.
The most serious criticism, of course, is that this Bill, while it goes a long way toward removing some of the really serious problems which many individuals have faced in the past, still excludes those individuals who have never been married; that

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act
is, the single pensioners. I know the Minister tried to head off some criticism in that area in his remarks. However, I believe it is still incumbent upon Members of the Opposition to point out in a very serious way that many of those individuals who are excluded are really having a hard time making ends meet, for a number of reasons which I will get into during my comments.
The Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith), in the course of his remarks, spoke very kindly about the former Member for Winnipeg North Centre, the Hon. Stanley Knowles, and the contribution he has made to the whole question of pension reform and, indeed, the structuring of the pension system in our country. In fact, I would even suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if any Hon. Member wishes to determine how pensions have been formulated in this country and how policy has been determined, the required reading would be the speeches of Stanley Knowles in the House and his questions and comments in the course of his political career. As a matter of fact that is what I have done, especially his speeches related to spouse's allowance. I went back quite a way and found that this is something which Mr. Knowles had concerned himself with over the years.
For the purposes of today's debate, however, I think it is sufficient to go back to the debate which took place in this Chamber on May 26, 1980. Mr. Knowles, with respect to the improvements, small as they were, to the pension system at that time, said: "While the movement has been good to improve pensions, we are still labouring under what I think is one of the most unfair pieces of social legislation ever introduced in this country, that is, the spouse's allowance". He went on to explain why he thought that was unfair. Later on, on the following day, Mr. Knowles said as reported at page 1456 of Hansard'.
Second, I ask the Minister, and I press this upon her as strongly as I can, whether in this term of office she is enjoying she is going to do something about the disgrace of the spouse's allowance legislation.
He went on to say that especially for women between the ages of 60 years and 65 years, for the most part there is applied a marital test. He continued:
If a woman has a man or has one that dies while she is in that age bracket, she gets the pension. But if she does not have a man because she is a spinster or divorced, or became a widow before age 60, or she became a widow before her husband was over 65, there is no pension there.
I read a speech that the Minister made last June in which he made much the same argument. It is to his credit that the first thing he did was to live up to the concerns which he expressed six or eight months ago. However, that still leaves a large number of women who are single, having never been married, without that extra amount of money which they could well use. Even at this late date as we go through committee perhaps we can still persuade the Minister and his Cabinet colleagues to do something for that large group of people.
I was surprised and a bit curious over the last week or two when I received two pieces of correspondence from a member of the former Government, the Hon. Member for Montreal-
Saint-Marie (Mr. Malepart), who expressed some anxiety and concern about that large group of single women who were excluded from this Bill. If the situation were not as serious as it is, I would find the flights of rhetoric used by this Member quite funny. I would simply ask the Hon. Member for Mont-real-Sainte-Marie where the hell he was over the years when Stanley Knowles was pressing the Government on this particular issue. I went through Hansard to see whether this particular individual was even mentioned as expressing a concern about this while he was a member of the Government. I could find no reference to it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I tried to find a reference too.

The Minister tried to find a reference also. We welcome the Hon. Member's support, albeit newly-found, while he is in opposition. However, I would be much more impressed by his arguments and concerns if, while he had an opportunity to do so, he had pressed the Government of which he was a member to do something about that inadequacy in the pension legislation.
I would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, if I did not say something about the present Government's previous commitment to pension reform and why it has not done something about it now that it forms the Government. I looked up Hansard for May 10, 1984. I read with some interest the motion that was put forward by the Progressive Conservative Party on that date, being an Opposition Day. I would feel comfortable moving that motion today, with a few changes in the dates, of course. For the interest of new Members in the House I will read the motion:
That this House profoundly regrets the two-year delay of the Government in bringing in promised legislation to improve guaranteed supplements for low-income single elderly Canadians, and condemns the Government for its failure to respond to the innovative proposals of the all-party Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform to expand opportunities for Canadians under age 65 to make adequate provision for income in their retirement years.
That motion was put forward by the present Government while it was in opposition on May 10, 1984. It was moved by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), the present Minister of Employment and Immigration. I know that that Minister feels strongly about the issue of pension reform. I wish her every success in lobbying and making her voice heard within Cabinet to bring forward the much-needed improvements which she spoke about in the course of her remarks on that Opposition Day. In fact, I intended to make much the same argument to the present Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The age-old argument is heard again. The Government says that it would love to bring in real pension reform for all senior citizens who gave their lives to make this country as great as it is, but it does not have the money. It says that it will make those improvements when the economy picks up and we are rolling in loot again. That argument has been made as far back as I can read in Hansard.
In 1951 an end was brought to the means test for old age pensions. At that time Stanley Knowles referred to debates that had gone on years and years before. The old argument
February 4, 1985

was used then as well. The Government said it would love to do something for pensioners but the country could not afford it.
I recall reading what Tommy Douglas, the former leader of my Party and the former Premier of Saskatchewan, said on the subject. He said that Governments have used that argument time and again until it is shop-worn. He said that Governments can never Find money for social programs to allow people to live with some social dignity in this world, but in order to finance a war they can grab oodles of money out of nowhere. I think the same arguments hold true at this time.
I would like to quote the comments made by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands on May 10, 1984. I am sure Members on the Government side will find this interesting. I certainly do. She said:
The fact that we have 600,000 elderly Canadians living in poverty in a country as rich and bountiful as Canada, in a society suppposedly as compassionate and humane as ours, is a national disgrace. The fact that this has been allowed to continue month after month, year after year, is a telling indictment of the Government. The Government is bereft of ideas, drained of decency, and unable to recognize the priorities which must be dealt with in this society. 1 know the Government has its priorities: bail-outs of de Havilland, Canadair and Maislin; bonuses for executive officers in de Havilland and the Canada Development Investment Corporation; and the purchase of Petrofina gas stations. We know what the priorities of the Government are. For the people who have, throughout their lifetimes, worked for and contributed to the development of this great country, there is only a promise trotted out time and time again that some day, some time, they too will become a priority.
Is it any wonder, Sir, that today we condemn the Government? We condemn it not only for its failure to introduce legislation that would meet the current needs of today's elderly poor, but also for its failure to bring about long overdue pension reform of the whole system so that we can ensure that the poverty of today will not be meted out to those who will be senior citizens in 10, 20 or 30 years' time. We must begin to come to grips with this issue and reverse what is happening.
I wish I had made that speech, Mr. Speaker, and I just did. The same arguments hold true today as they did on May 10, 1984, during the debate in 1951, and during the debate in the early 1930s when pensions first began to be spoken about seriously by the decision-makers in this and other countries. It is time that the Government did something about it rather than talk. When the Minister tabled the child and elderly benefits consultation paper, I thought he would have taken the opportunity to say something serious about this topic. I have no doubt that the Minister is a sincere person. The Minister is a man with integrity and I thought he would have taken the opportunity to say something serious about pension reform.
However, he said in his paper that while not proposing changes at this time in the elderly benefits system, the Government invites proposals and comments regarding the age exemption and the pension income deduction, the elderly benefits system and so on. We do not need another study on pension reform because the issue has been studied to death over the years.
I was an alternate to my former colleague, Ted Miller, on the Pension Reform Task Force. Incidentally, I also want to congratulate that committee for dealing with a very difficult and complex subject and proposing the recommendations that
Old Age Security Act
it did, even though I disagree with some of them. I believe the committee could have made stronger recommendations on some of the issues it was studying. In any event, I believe it is time for real pension reform in this country.
I would be remiss if I did not also mention the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) who, two years ago, headed our Party's task force to look into the problems of older women across the country. She issued a very impressive document as a result of those investigations and I would be more than happy to provide the Minister with a copy if he has not seen the document. I believe it deals with these problems in a very human, warm and compassionate way.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is appropriate that I end my remarks by referring to some statements which have been made by the Council on Pension Reform for Singles. The Hon. Member for Sudbury may recall that Miss Cheevers, the secretary of that Council, appeared before the Task Force on Pension Reform and gave testimony that astounded everyone in the room at that particular time. Miss Cheevers is a woman in her late seventies, I believe. She was brought up in an era when the money that was available to a family usually went to the male in order to provide him with an education.
This was her testimony at the hearing. She said that there were two children in her family, herself and her brother. It was assumed that since there was a shortage of money at the time and that only one of the two children could receive an education, her brother would receive the education because he would eventually be the breadwinner. Miss Cheevers was denied the right to an education because of the lack of money in the family. It was expected that she would grow up to be married and raise children in the usual stereotype situation that we would not accept today.
The First World War broke out when Miss Cheevers was growing up. Most of the males in Canada who went overseas returned with spouses and many never returned. According to Miss Cheevers, this is one reason why she never married. Not only was she involved in the war effort at home, but her parents had become elderly by the time the war was over. Since she was expected to look after her parents she did not enter the workforce until she was in her mid-fifties. She did not have an opportunity to make contributions to a private pension plan and it was too late for her to make contributions to the Canada Pension Plan. Registered retirement savings plans were of no use to her because she did not have an income that would allow her to buy an RRSP. What happened to Miss Cheevers and thousands like her who are members of this Council is that they are now living on a very meagre pension. They are excluded by this legislation that is being brought forward by the Minister and they are having a hard time to make ends meet in this country.
Let me quote from a newsletter that was issued by the Council on Pension Reform for Singles. It says more than I can say because these people are speaking from their own experience. I am sure Members will be interested to hear what they have to say:

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act
In the last administration it was the Minister responsible for the Status of Women who said that singles who had not married and not had children and contributed nothing to Canada. With that kind of representation who needs enemies?
Our kind friend should have been around during two great wars and a real depression, 18 years out of what should have been the most productive period of their lives when it was the single women who turned in to keep the home fires burning and were acclaimed as heroes and the backbone of Canada. In those days we did not advocate leaving the country helpless against the enemy. We had to defend it and did so with every ounce we possessed. There being no men left to marry following the wars, they turned in to support their war widowed mothers and young brothers and sisters, only to find that a grateful Canada has abandoned them pension wise as though they don't exist-
We know what we are talking about. We are of an age who went through it all and we feel that we have as much reason to be proud of our achievements as any women who sits in the House of Commons and it is time we were recognized. There are not many years left.
Having got off our chests that which has been choking us so long, dare we hope that the House of Commons members will take the time to do some homework by reading and learning something about the roots of Old Age Security. It is very evident they need the education.
I think that sums up any contribution I have to make to this debate. I wish the Minister well. If Members of my Party can be of assistance to him in pressuring other members of his Cabinet, he will always have our support and I hope he will use it and act as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate the Minister on this overdue Bill. Let me also congratulate the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) and the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) for adopting a reasonable attitude in this debate. This may be one of the rare days in the House when we will take the action that the country has asked for with a minimum of rancour.
I have been a long time supporter of pensioners, veterans and other Canadians who have found themselves disadvantaged by the sins of omission or commission in various forms of our legislation. I heartily welcome the progressive initiative taken by the present Government.
I am pleased to have this opportunity, my first in this Parliament, to speak on this topic. The main purpose of this Bill is to broaden the eligibility of widows and widowers in financial need for a spouse's allowance by allowing applications to be made by a surviving spouse between the ages of 60 and 64, regardless of the age of the deceased partner.
The spouse's allowance was first introduced into the Old Age Security Act in a 1975 amendment. Since that time its scope has been extended on four other occasions, making this the fifth amendment relating directly to the spouse's allowance.
While this amendment is not discriminatory-men and women are both able to benefit-by far the largest beneficiaries will be women. For some reason unknown to me but adequately supported by statistics, women tend to outlive men and therefore many more of them will receive assistance as a result of the amendment. Our Government maintains a commitment to ensure the legislation in this and other areas reflects accurately the needs of the population. It is progressive legislation.
In my 12 years in Parliament on both sides of the House I have advocated, with the full support of my colleagues, several important issues along the same lines as this amendment to the Old Age Security Act. In each instance an injustice had been brought about by legislation which was too restrictive or did not address the problem that had arisen. Now that we are in a position to implement the progressive measures that we have proposed over the years, I am sure the Canadian public can expect many more. Indeed, the Speech from the Throne outlined measures which are outlined expressly "to ensure that social measures in Canada keep pace with the changing needs and circumstances of our people".
I, too, would like to mention two former Members of this House who shared my concerns about the inequities of legislation, especially that affecting pensioners and their spouses. The first is the late Hon. Walter Baker. He was a tireless worker who, with his obvious legal skills, combined with large doses of compassion, spoke often about the needs of pensioners and about the lack of will demonstrated by the former Government to amend legislation to remove certain inequities. 1 am sure he would be sharing my enthusiasm for this amendment to the Old Age Security Act if he were here.
The other former Member who has been mentioned by everyone preceding me this morning and who still graces the House with his presence at the Table at times is, of course, known far and wide for his interest and advocacy on behalf of pensioners and veterans. I am referring, of course, to the Hon. Stanley Knowles. Incidentally, he was a great help to me as a new Member many years ago with his advice on all pension matters. Throughout his decades here as the Member for Winnipeg North Centre he was always a champion and watchdog of government. He did not miss an opportunity to remind the government of the day of its obligations to the people who worked and fought for the rest of us and then found their government less than generous in providing for their retirement years. I shall do my best, along with other colleagues who share these concerns, to continue that tradition.
My constituency, Victoria, has almost 89,000 individuals living and, my notes say, working in it. Unfortunately, a very large number are no longer working because of the difficult economic times that we have. Of the 89,000 people, a very significant proportion are over the age of 60. As a matter of fact, 29,000 or 32 per cent of the population of Victoria are over 60. Of that percentage, about 61 per cent are women.
It was, therefore, a great day when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) tabled the discussion paper on elderly and family benefits. The paper has reinforced the concept of universality for elderly benefits by stating that removing universality is not an option being considered by our Government. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), in the days leading up to the election, promised that. The Government has repeatedly maintained its commitment in this Parliament and now the Minister has confirmed that commitment.
February 4, 1985

In a statement last November, the Minister said:
-our goal is to strengthen the integrity of universality, its goal of comprehensiveness and fairness ... Canadians have never had a version of universality in which the theory and the reality are absolutely the same.
My constituents can be assured of continuing benefits which they richly deserve, as indeed do all elderly Canadians.
This Old Age Security Act amendment is only the latest in a series of progressive legislative initiatives which my Party has supported. One in which I was proud to have played a part was that involving pensions for those who defended our country during past wars and their spouses. In fact, the last time I spoke on this side of the House in favour of a Government Bill was on my own Bill on this very subject. While I was Minister of Veterans Affairs in the 1979-80 Conservative Government, I was privileged to introduce, with the support of my colleagues, amending legislation which applied to the Pension Act, the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act.
Among other things, that Bill, which was Bill C-28, did away with two previously ignored inequities. First, it provided the widow of a veteran who had been in receipt of a disability pension of less than 48 per cent with a proportionate pension. Up to that time the widow had been unable to claim a dime if the disability pension had been less than 48 per cent. Second, the other significant change in that legislation was to provisions of the Veterans Land Act. Previously, the spouse of a veteran had not been entitled to any interest in land acquired by a veteran under the Act and court orders were ignored by the director of the Veterans Land Act administration. With the passage of that amendment the spouse would be able to make application through the courts for an interest in the veteran's property, and the Director would be obliged to take notice of the claim. It is hard to believe that a provision such as this was not even considered prior to 1979. In any event, our Government came to an end two days after introduction of the Bill so I was unable to see it come to fruition at that time. I was thankful it was adopted by the succeeding government as Bill C-40 and given speedy passage, and it is now the law of the land.
In 1982 there was another Bill of this nature introduced in Parliament and passed without much fanfare at the time. This Bill was entitled Garnishment, Attachment and Pension Diversion Act. However, proclamation of Parts II, III and IV of the Act were inordinately delayed. The purpose of the legislation was two-fold: to remove constraints against public servants being garnisheed and to allow spouses to obtain direct from the Government all or part of a public servant's pay or pension where there is a court order for family maintenance. The intent of this portion of the legislation was to circumvent difficulties some spouses had and were having in collecting maintenance orders. This sort of thing was leaving them in precarious financial circumstances. Seventeen months later this Act still had not been proclaimed, leaving many spouses who were anticipating proclamation swaying in the wind.
At that time I proceeded by way of correspondence, questions and speeches.in the House to have the problem resolved,
Old Age Security Act
which was finally done by passage of a second Bill. I expect that some of the senior staff of the House of Commons are more aware of what held up the proclamation of Bill C-35 than I am. Eventually, the impasse was resolved by the passage of an additional Bill which said that yes, employees of the House of Commons would have to come under the provisions of the Bill as passed by the House of Commons.
That is a brief record of the Party's and my own position on legislative initiatives in the same vein as those before us today. Anomalies and inequities will continue to be revealed in our legislation. The reasons they occur are legion, but I believe those relating to changes in social attitudes are slowly but surely coming to be recognized and omitted.
Once again, may I read from the Speech from the Throne two statements to confirm our commitment to social equality:
-there is some distance between the principle of equality, widely accepted, and its reality, still far short of achievement. It is the duty of Parliament and Government to help ensure that Canadian society travels that distance as quickly as possible.
Further on in the Speech we find:
Canadians value and support the comprehensive social security system that has been put in place over many years... Many areas of the system must be strengthened to respond to the changing nature and needs of our society.
What is much more difficult to bring to light are those inequities created by our economic situation, a situation created in large part by profligate spending by our predecessors, an economy shaped by political expediency, short-sightedness and reactionary measures. Now that the Conservative Party has an unambiguous mandate from Canadians to set to right the damage inflicted over the last 16 years on our economy, this legislation is proof that it will be done judiciously. It is proof that our Party will cure our society's economic ailments while at the same time ensuring protection and fairness to those whose finances are limited.
Hear, hear!

Our Government is fortunate to have the present Minister of National Health and Welfare, who is known for his compassion, sense of fairness, and capability. I am confident that this needed amendment is a harbinger of further equitable legislation. Canada's elderly citizens can share my confidence.
There are some parts of Bill C-26 which are somewhat puzzling. I realize that the committee is the place in which to study the Bill very carefully and either have its parts satisfactorily explained or changed. I am rather concerned about Clause 1(1) which defines a spouse and about the part which speaks of the bar to remarriage. I trust in committee we will ensure that we are not making moral judgments or reinforcing a moralistic attitude by denying funds to people who need them just as much as if they were the most moral people in the world. I do not think it is a part of federal legislation to set out absolute moral lines as to who can qualify.

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act
I should like to see other legislation come on stream. Now there is a possibility of this. I look forward to the day when we might be equal to the country of Belgium which has a pension for women at age 60. It would ensure that inequities would not be disclosed only after legislation is put into effect. At the present time, and even after this Bill is passed, in the case of 62-year old twin sisters, one will be able to draw this pension because she was married and the other will not. That does not seem fair, but the facts of the Bill are generally pleasing. As I understand the Bill, with zero income the monthly payment will be $536.26. This will be gradually reduced. If there is outside income, it will have to go over $10,500 before the allowance will be cut out completely. It is an understanding Bill.
In summary, my wholehearted support for this legislation is what I wish to express. It is an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act. It derives from its compassionate nature. It addresses some of the issues about which we care a great deal-those issues affecting elderly Canadians, in particular women. I hope my colleagues on both sides of the House will share my enthusiasm for this Bill and give it quick passage so that its benefits can proceed without undue delay.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there questions or comments on the Hon. Member's speech? If not, we shall resume debate with the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone).

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to address the issue of spousal allowance and applaud the decision of the Minister in this regard. The Government is extending this benefit to help an estimated 85,000 elderly widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 65 regardless of when their spouses died. For this group it is an excellent first step. I support this measure in the hope that it will evolve even further and that at some point in time we will be able to consider the 80,000 to 85,000 who are left out of the provisions of this particular Bill. I am sure the Minister felt as badly as I do in having to exclude this segment of single elderly Canadians from the proposal. The prospect of poverty for them is very real and very frightening. I am sure the Minister shares that concern.

I want to congratulate the Minister on presenting this legislation, which is in the best interests of all Canadians. We do not intend to oppose the passage of a Bill that was examined by a task force set up under the previous Government. The task force was headed by one of our Members, the Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith). Incidentally, this Government is introducing quite a number of Liberal measures and seems to be abandoning the reactionary Conservative measures advocated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). I am delighted that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has been able to make his contribution to the wellbeing of our society.

I am basically very concerned because I believe it is often the case when we talk about these kinds of measures that we really do not stop to think of them in terms of a total portrait or picture. We often say that all these measures are from the bleeding hearts of society and that we cannot afford them. What we really cannot afford is a society which allows people to live in abject poverty. This has an impact upon their families, their children and themselves. In the long run this is very costly to society.
I should like to tell a story about my friend Jeanne. She is in her late fifties. She works in a large company. Her task is to train employees to run computerized machines. She earns about $18,000 per year. She considered herself well paid at one point, but now she has come to certain realities. After 12 years on this job, other men and women start with the company as clerks and secretaries with salaries of $19,000 to $21,000 in their first year. This seems unfair to Jeanne, and it is. What is even more unfair is that the men she trains for the job are immediately put into higher positions than hers. They are promoted and receive higher salaries, and she has trained them.
She would like to fight the system in order to be treated more fairly, but she is afraid she will lose her job. She does not think she could get another job because she is too old. She has no other income and no pension. She cannot change the world alone. She needs all our help as legislators.
I should like to suggest that the Canadian economy and the subject of women's income is one and the same thing, in a sense. I will be told that these are two separate issues, not one issue. I believe that for far too long women's issues and issues related to the Canadian economy have been considered separately when in fact they are one issue. Too often political and business leaders, economists and public officials say: "Today I will take a speech and talk about women. Tomorrow I will talk about social policy. Then maybe on Friday I will outline our economic policy". To treat the income problems of more than half the population separately from major economic questions is to short-change women, for their role, welfare and wellbeing are synonymous with economic and social policy. I am quite pleased to note that in the economic summit which the Government is planning the voice of women will be heard. It is almost too late, but certainly it is a step forward.
The reality is that today and for too long women in Canada have been losing out economically. The harsh fact is that two-thirds of Canadians working at the minimum wage level are women. The startling fact is that over half of all Canadian women can expect to be poor at some point in their lives. Another sad fact is that 2.5 times as many women as men are forced into part-time work because that is all they can find. The bitter fact is that when couples separate, although a man can generally look forward to rising income the woman anticipates only diminishing income. Only 27 per cent of employed women are enrolled in private pension plans and only one out of four widows has a pension. To quote one of the great North
February 4, 1985

American Liberals, "When is a buck not a buck?" It is when a woman earns it and it is only worth 62 cents.
Now, some will say: "There she goes again, talking about spending taxpayers' money on social policy". I have discovered that the real difference between social policy and economic policy is when someone else is describing the life of a single woman working and raising a family on a minimum wage or a woman without any income at all. When we talk about that, we are talking about social policy. If you happen to be that woman who is living on the minimum wage or has no income at all, what is happening to you is an economic reality.
It is time to change economic realities. It is time to act. It is time to devise and implement a national economic policy that counts women in rather than dealing them out. We must make a commitment to end the historic economic injustices that have been done to women in this country. We must make a commitment to the working women of Canada, those who want to work outside of their homes and those who have no choice but to work outside their homes.
If you go to work in Canada to support your family and yourself and contribute to the wealth of this country, you will receive equal pay for work of equal value. We cannot wait. We must commit ourselves to action now. We must do nothing less. That is fairness and equity. We must start with the premise that in the workplace women are not different from men in their abilities, in their energies, in their drive to work and in what they can produce for their families and for the nation.
We must accept the fact that many women are not paid fairly for what they do. This inequity is found at all levels of income. It is also true for women with university educations. For example, women who have MBAs who started with the same salary as men find they are thousands of dollars behind their classmates in a few short years. Therefore, we must act now.
The federal Government must pay its employees equal pay for work of equal value. We must be pro-active in this matter and lead the reform, not simply leave the onus on those who feel that they have a grievance. The federal Government should contract only with Canadian companies, professional firms or institutions that provide to its employees equal pay for work of equal value.
There are those who would argue that such policies must be gradual and depend on a growing economic tie in Canada. We can work at being just if we just get a bigger economic growth, a bigger pie to share and to cut.
Exactly.
I am glad to see the Minister in the House.
I have been here all along. Where have you been?

I have been here. I just looked your way.

The economic boom of the 1960s and 1970s proved that this was not the case. While the nation's wealth grew dramatically, the gap between the incomes of women and men did not close. Whether the Canadian economic pie gets bigger, and we are all working to ensure that it does, or smaller, which I doubt, or remains static, which is the fear of some, whatever the size of that pie we must divide it more fairly. The slice women have had has not been a fair slice, and it should be.
In addition to a commitment for equal pay for work of equal value, which I know the Minister is presently studying-and I await with a great deal of interest her reaction and that of her ministry to the Abella commission-there are two other areas where we can act.
As a person who feels that there is a tremendous need to see increased equity, we must act to help the low-income single head of the household who is raising children. We must do more to help Canadian women in their late fifties and sixties who suddenly lose all sources of income. The action undertaken by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) is one step. I mentioned the other which I hope some day we can realize.
Allow me to deal first with the major economic question of women who are single heads of households, unable to work or working at the minimum wage or not much more. The situation in Canada is that there are over 580,000 Canadian women today who are single heads of households. Forty one per cent of these women live below the poverty line. Most who have married and are now separated are unable to enforce child maintenance orders. In fact, only 30 per cent are receiving the awards allocated to them. What is more, the trend in our country is that half of those who marry under the age of 30 will separate. If we do nothing, we will see a worsening situation in which women find themselves. Three out of four women in Canada either do not marry or lose their husbands through death, divorce or separation.
In my talks with women and women's groups, I have been told the same story over and over again. It is the story of a single person with a minimum wage. Most of those people are women who must pay rent, feed and clothe their families, pay their own transportation and look for daycare. The harsh reality is that she cannot stretch that minimum wage to cover the rent, food, clothing, transportation and daycare. That amount of income just will not cover the cost of the basics.
The question is what do we do for women faced with this situation? I do not have all the answers, but I ask Hon. Members to consider what is happening when women are forced to quit. We lose her productivity and her work outside the home. We lose her contribution to the economy. We pay the welfare costs for being at home and out of the workforce. We destroy the spirit of one more Canadian who has given in and given up on herself and on society. There has to be another way. I think it is a lack of political will sometimes to resolve to meet these problems and find answers.
Let me turn to the second group of Canadian women who require change in our economic policies. I speak of the woman who has never been in the workforce but who has had to work

all her life in her home. She is a worker and by working with her family she has contributed enormously to the social and economic infrastructure of Canada.
