We must work at all the economic issues in Canada and, as politicians, we must also have priorities and the courage to pursue them boldly. I urge action in these most pressing areas because action will help those Canadians who need it most now. I urge the implementation of a new economic policy for all Canadians but one that will create greater income for women. That is why I urge a vigorous pursuit of a policy of equal pay for work of equal value, of income support for low wage single heads of households and of a basic income for Canadians and especially women in their late fifties and early sixties who have been forced into an incomeless life. Motherhood is enhanced, and it places equal value on women who stay in the home, nurturing their children, as on those who work in the marketplace.

February 4, 1985

the Minister give the Quebec Minister of Industry and Trade a chance to make offers that might attract this industry to Quebec, at a time when the heartland of Quebec and the province in general have lost thousands of jobs since the Conservatives came to power?

subsubtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-IMPORTANCE OF SETTLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister my question is for the Minister responsible for Multiculturalism. The Minister will know that yesterday the President of the National Association of Japanese Canadians met with the executive of that body, and that they in turn reconfirmed their confidence in the approach that he has been taking on their behalf in meetings with the Government of Canada.
It is of profound importance that we reach a settlement on this important tragedy in the history of our country which all Parties in the House can accept and agree upon, and more important, that the Japanese Canadians will feel at home with. Will the Minister assure the House that he will follow up on Mr. Miki's request to meet with the Prime Minister, by urging that the Prime Minister agree to such a meeting?

subsubtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-IMPORTANCE OF SETTLEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, obviously I cannot speak for the Prime Minister in terms of whom he will and will not meet. I have indicated to Mr. Miki and any other members of the Japanese community that I am prepared to meet with them at any time they see fit to discuss this very important matter further. My offer and invitation still stand.

Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House thank the Minister for his reply. Will he also indicate clearly to the House that the Government is willing to fulfil its own previous commitment to have serious negotiations with representatives of the Japanese Canadian community before any particular matter is brought before the House for the purpose of agreement?

Mr. Speaker, my reply to the Hon. Member will be roughly the same as my first reply. I am prepared to sit down and discuss this matter with the Japanese community at any time. They understand that. I would expect some overtures by Mr. Miki and his group this week. If that takes place, I will be prepared to sit down and talk about any matters that may arise from one end of the spectrum to the other.

Mr. Speaker, from past discussions on this matter, which have taken place both in and outside the House, the Minister knows that there is an important distinction to be made between the terms" consultation" and "negotiation". Is the Minister now prepared to say that the Government will continue with the negotiating process on this important matter before any legislation or resolution is brought before Parliament?
February 4, 1985

Mr. Speaker, I have communicated to the Japanese Canadian community that I am prepared to have discussions. One of my major concerns is that, if we get into a negotiating position, which I understand some members of the Japanese Canadian community would like to see, with their lawyer representatives at the table, that inherently puts us into more of a confrontational type of position. I want to try to do everything in my power to stay away from that. I would like to have the question discussed at great length, if necessary, so that both sides are firm in their understanding of the direction we should go. I do not think it would be in the best interest of either side to sit down and start to negotiate, as such, at the present time.
I am very much concerned, as I know the Hon. Member would be, that it could lead to more confrontation.

subsubtopic: GENERAL MOTORS' SEARCH FOR NEW PLANT LOCATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. Recently General Motors announced that it was looking for a site for a $3.5 billion assembly plant for its new Saturn project. It is also known that some 19 Governors of States in the United States are pressing to have that plant located in their areas. Exactly what are the Minister and his officials doing to get that plant located right here in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Sinclair Stevens (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
subsubtopic: GENERAL MOTORS' SEARCH FOR NEW PLANT LOCATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to assure the Hon. Member for Windsor West that we are very much in touch with the officials in the Canadian head office of General Motors, as well as in Detroit. We are working with the provinces and federal officials to ensure that Canada is considered and hopefully will be able to win the type of development that General Motors is talking about.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, how can the Minister realistically expect to have any chance to get that plant located in Canada when, in the face of very extensive incentives being offered to General Motors by the 19 State Governors I have mentioned, to have the plant located in their areas, he and his Government have reduced support for the auto industry that was previously available to it through the Industrial and Regional Development Program? Will he not agree now that he must reverse those cuts if he is to have any chance of getting that plant located in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Sinclair Stevens (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I suggest to the Hon. Member that he get a better researcher, because the fact is that this Government has in no way reduced the amount of funds that are available under the Industrial and Regional Development
Oral Questions
Program. In fact those that might be available to help the auto industry are very much still available.
As the Hon. Member must recall, when it was proposed that General Motors put a substantial plant at Ste. Therese, Quebec, of course we were there offering assistance, along with the Province of Quebec. We would do so in the future if it meant more jobs for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It concerns the discussions with respect to renegotiation of the NORAD Treaty. As the Minister knows, in 1981 the previous Liberal Government deleted the clause dealing with the ABMs, thus paving the way potentially for our entry into star wars. Would the Secretary of State assure the House today that, in the negotiations taking place now and in the weeks to come, his Government will make it abundantly clear to the Americans that we want that clause put back in, and thereby prevent us from getting involved in an offensive star wars program?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is correct when he points out that there was a deletion of a clause. I have naturally inquired as to why the Liberal Government agreed to that deletion at that particular time. I am informed that, in fact, that particular clause was deleted precisely to avoid any suggestion that either Canada or the United States might take actions which would breach the ABM Treaty.
I would be prepared to discuss that matter at greater length with the Hon. Member, with others in the House who are interested, or to make officials available.
To the best of my understanding, after inquiries, that was the reason for that clause being deleted. Consequently, I would be surprised if Members of the House who are anxious to have the ABM Treaty respected would want to reinsert a clause which might contain the suggestion that it would open the way for the United States to depart from the obligations of that treaty.

Mr. Speaker, I find the logic a little difficult to follow. I believe the only way to clear this matter up is to ask the Secretary of State if he will undertake to make sure that the complete NORAD Agreement is brought before the House Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence for complete examination before it is signed by anyone, either on this side of the border or the American side of the border?

February 4, 1985
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will be aware that there was a recommendation from the Standing Committee a year or two ago calling for a review of the NORAD arrangement prior to its renewal. Its renewal occurs in March of next year, which is more than a year away.
The Hon. Member will know that there will be a reference to the committees of Parliament of both a white paper from the Department of National Defence and a green paper from External Affairs, which will cover those questions, among others. If parliamentarians, after seeing those papers, conclude that that does not provide an adequate opportunity for that kind of study, the Government certainly will be prepared to consider any requests for any further opportunities to ensure that there is wide public understanding of all of the implications of renewal of the NORAD Agreement 13 months hence.

speechtext: May I interrupt proceedings to advise Members of the presence in our gallery today of the Hon. Lome Hepworth, Minister of Agriculture for the Province of Saskatchewan.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General, and it concerns the Richard Hatfield marijuana case. In view of today's press reports and the many questions that have been raised about this case, will the Solicitor General initiate a complete and independent review of the investigation and prosecution of the case so that the public can be assured that our criminal justice system has worked fairly and objectively in the matter?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the Hon. Member's question. At this time I must respectfully decline to give any such assurance.

Mr. Speaker, my question, which is directed to the Minister of Transport, concerns the remarks made by the Prime Minister on Friday about acid rain and the need for Canadians to clean up their own backyard before we can negotiate from strength with the Americans.
Will the Minister tell us today, in keeping with the spirit of the Prime Minister's remarks, whether Canada will soon move to adopt the recommendation of the parliamentary subcommittee on acid rain that the current standard of 3.1 grams per vehicle mile be tightened to one gram per vehicle mile, which is the current U.S. standard with regard to emissions of nitrous oxide?
Mr. Speaker, that is a matter that is currently under active consideration by myself and Cabinet colleagues. Of course, we will be cognizant of the statements made by the Prime Minister on Friday.

Mr. Speaker, could the Minister be more definite? He knows that he must make this announcement by April 1 if it is to take effect by the 1987 car model year.
Could he give us assurances that he will make that announcement before April 1-indeed before President Reagan's visit-so that the Prime Minister would be able to point to some concrete Canadian action in his discussions with the President of the United States about acid rain?

Mr. Speaker, any announcement relative to exhaust emissions will be made in due course.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Could he clarify the $30 million cut-back to the Medical Research Council's budget? Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. There has been widespread concern, expressed by agricultural groups such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the National Farmers' Union, about the cut-backs in Canagrex. For instance, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture stated in its brief to the Minister last week that it was angered and surprised by that Minister's and the Minister of Finance's arbitrary action.
Also, in view of the tremendous success this corporation has had in its first year when it sold over $16 million worth of farm products, and has another $160 million under consideration, would the Minister be prepared to reconsider his decision and allow this corporation another year of operation to prove that it actually can improve on its first year's successes?
Mr. Speaker, in response to the Hon. Member's question, I must indicate to him that, as far as I am concerned, and as far as this Government is concerned, Canagrex is really history.
Hear, hear!

The Hon. Member should know that since the Government took the decision with reference to Canagrex I have been in a position to receive representations of all kinds from all regions of the country. Other than the two or three exceptions which the Hon. Member has mentioned, the vast majority of representations that I have received have all been positively in support of the decision taken by the Government.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the Minister does not know what the two national farm organizations are. I am referring to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the National Farmers' Union.
Let me ask the Minister of Agriculture why it is, when the United States and the EEC countries are more aggressively marketing and selling agricultural commodities, that we are shutting down the one organization that is set up to sell our commodities abroad? Why is it that we are going in one direction while very other country in the world is more aggressively marketing farm commodities?

Mr. Speaker, I want to make it very clear that this Government will very aggressively follow the export market for agricultural commodities. We are satisfied, given that very dismal record of Canagrex, that we can do it far more successfully, far more efficiently and effectively, with officials in my Department. Indeed, some reorganization has already begun, and we do not need an additional Crown corporation to provide the much needed export guarantee package. Our Department has already entered into negotiations and had discussions and that role will be carried on more effectively and more successfully with the Export Development Corporation properly financed.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs. I would like to thank him for his help to date. As he is well aware, a Canadian citizen Mr. Roberto Starita, of Prince Rupert, has been held by the Brazilian police at the Praca Maua Prison in Rio de Janiero for three weeks now, without charges. Since Mr. Starita was recognized by the United Nations as a political refugee in 1977, at which time he was in Brazil, has the Minister taken any steps with the United Nations in attempting to secure his immediate release and return to Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have taken no steps with the United Nations yet, but the Hon. Member will know that, due to his own very active intervention in the case, and his contact with me and with my officials, representatives of the Canadian Embassy have been in touch regularly with Mr. Starita, and we are doing everything we can to ensure his security and to prevent any worsening of his situation. If it appears to be appropriate that we make appeals to other bodies, we will do that.

February 4, 1985
Oral Questions CONDITIONS OF DETENTION

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs. Since the Brazilian authorities are content to hold Mr. Starita in a windowless, black cage, without even sanitary facilities, without charge and without trial, does the Minister not think it is about time to place a call to the new President-elect of Brazil, Mr. Neves, to protest vigorously to him about this abuse of a Canadian citizen?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

Mr. Speaker, we will consider any action that would be productive and helpful in easing this situation. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. In his 1983-84 annual report, the Auditor General referred to a serious problem in Public Service job classifications. He pointed out that 19 per cent of Public Service positions were overclassified, at very high cost to the taxpayer. When my colleague from Windsor West was President of the Treasury Board, he announced serious measures aimed at correcting this overclassification. Could the Minister inform the House what he has done and what he intends to do to deal with this very serious problem?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as job classifications in the Public Service are concerned, the Government generally agrees with what the Auditor General said in his annual report. In fact, all this was already very obvious from the Treasury Board's own audits in
1983.	Corrective action was taken in 1984, and the situation has improved considerably. I can assure the Hon. Member that I intend to keep a very close watch on the process to ensure that the new measures are indeed being effective.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the countless election promises made by the Conservative Party was that staffing procedures, classification, technological change, designations, and other issues would be made negotiable in public service contracts in the future. negotiated with the Public Service Alliance or with public service unions in general, job classification will be made negotiable?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have been meeting on those election promises which the Hon. Member mentioned.
Do you find the time?

Yes, I try to find time. I have been meeting very regularly with our labour leaders. We have had a number of meetings over the past few months and I am happy to report to the Hon. Member that we are making some very interesting progress on all six issues that we are discussing at the moment.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. It has to do with the recent tour of the NDP action group on jobs in Atlantic Canada and in western Canada. During that tour, business groups and individuals on many occasions brought to our attention that the present government purchasing policy discriminates against businesses in Atlantic Canada and western Canada, since less than 15 per cent of all government purchasing now comes from Atlantic Canada in combination with western Canada.
Considering that discriminatory purchasing policy is in place, and considering the need for jobs in both of those areas, is the Minister prepared to consider placing targets for government purchasing in those two regions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Sinclair Stevens (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in reply to the Hon. Member I would like to assure him that it also concerns us that there is not more purchasing as far as government procurement is concerned in regions such as the west, including British Columbia, and Atlantic Canada. I do not know whether it is fair to say it is a discriminatory practice. I think what is needed are more measures to ensure that whatever opportunities there are, are known to the local businessmen so that they can at least bid on the business. If the setting of targets, as the Hon. Member has suggested, would help, we will look at that. If, in order to encourage it, the greater selling and the buying of products in regions such as Atlantic Canada and the western areas would be helped by the setting of quotas, we will do it.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of State for Small Businesses. He, on many occasions, has indicated that
February 4, 1985

90 per cent of jobs created in Canada are being created by the small business sector.
Considering that 90 per cent of new jobs are created in the small business sector, the Minister will be aware that less than 30 per cent of all government procurement comes from the small business sector. Is he prepared to consider setting targets and government purchasing policies to assist small business, to assist the real job-creation sector of the country?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. A tax court decision recently resulted in an unemployment insurance overpayment to about 350 persons. In one case an individual owes an overpayment of $40,000. Is the Minister prepared to review the situation and exercise ministerial discretion and consider for unemployment insurance purposes only that these individuals, between 1978 and 1982, were indeed covered under the Unemployment Insurance Act?

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem to which the Hon. Member refers has arisen as a result of a court ruling that reversed the previous legislation. As a result, once the court had ruled, individuals were not able from then on either to pay into the unemployment insurance fund or to draw benefits from it. If they had, as has happened in this case, the Unemployment Insurance Commission is required by law, under the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act, to pay back moneys which were paid in improperly, and to retrieve benefits which were paid out improperly.
However, I inform the Hon. Member that if these payments are to be retrieved, it must be done in a fair and humane way. I have instructed that anyone who is on unemployment insurance, welfare, or in that sort of situation, must not be asked for repayment at this time.

Mr. Speaker, would the Minister consider changing the law-and she has our commitment on this side of the House that we will give it speedy passage-to alleviate the pressure and stress which are being brought to bear on many of these families? Can the Minister assure us that she will bring in a law which will put them onside and avoid the overpayments?

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will certainly give the suggestion that has been put forward by the Hon. Member every consideration. I understand the concern that he expresses. I want to assure him that, at the moment, under the terms of the legislation both I and the Commission have very little discretion with which to act.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all Members of the House agree that this is a
very important subject that we are discussing today. There are many ramifications that should be raised in addition to the specific parameters of the Bill. I would like particularly to speak to those in my remarks.
When he spoke this morning, the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) presented the New Democratic Party position with regard to Bill C-26. We will not oppose this Bill since it extends benefits to widows and widowers. It also includes common law partners who have lived together for three or more years. It corrects some of the language which was sexist.
We will not unduly delay this Bill. However, we would like to speak out again on how limited the coverage of this Bill is, considering the needs of older citizens, particularly those aged 60 to 65. While the Government has removed the sexist language, and we do not object to that, by the nature of the Bill and the limitation of its coverage it continues to practice sexual discrimination against single persons 60 to 65.
The former Member for Winnipeg North Centre, now sitting at the Table, the Hon. Stanley Knowles, stated many times in this House that spousal allowance legislation is sexist. It discriminates against single people. It requires that a man or a woman must live with a partner in order to qualify for the special allowances. There is a glaring omission in the Bill which discriminates against single persons aged 60 to 65, of which there are many in our society today. Statistics Canada estimates that 10 per cent or one in 10 women between the ages of 60 and 64 years are single or divorced.
The task force on older women which this Party conducted several years ago stated that these people in society are the poorest and least secure financially. The number of women in this age bracket has more than doubled since 1971. Women are the poorest of the poor in our society. In many cases they are much worse off than women aged 65 who at least receive the old age pension.
I again remind the House that the Hon. Stanley Knowles spoke to this matter repeatedly. I would like to remind the new Members of the House of one of the speeches he made on May 26, 1980, in regard to this matter. As reported on page 1400 of Hansard, he said:
I want to speak about some of the groups that are still left without the consideration and the attention they deserve. That group consists mainly of women who are alone or unattached. A good deal has been said about this $35 supplement that we are going to give now, and are giving in many cases to single women.... But we are still labouring under what I think is one of the most unfair pieces of social legislation we have ever produced in this country, and that is the spouse's allowance. No amount of trying to fix it up, as the former Liberal government did just before it was defeated or as the Conservative government did while it was in power, got us away from the fact that the spouse's allowance continues to be an unfair arrangement, f know this works both ways; it applies to men if they are the younger ones, but there are not that many of them.
I would say that there are more such men at this time than the Hon. Member may have realized in 1980. He went on:
According to this arrangement, women in the age bracket 60 to 65 who might be in need get no consideration at all unless they are married to, and living with, an older spouse. The woman in that age bracket who is a widow, divorced or single receives no consideration at all. I know there are a few cases of women in
February 4, 1985

that age bracket who were spouses and were receiving the spouse's allowance but then lost their husbands and now receive the spouse's allowance until they are 65 years of age. That touches only a small part of the problem.
Mr. Stanley Knowles went on to say:
The only way that it can be corrected is by providing whatever you are going to provide to the spouse between the ages of 60 and 65 without regard to marital status.
I would stress that, Mr. Speaker. I wish the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) would hear this. These allowances should be provided regardless of marital status. Mr. Knowles went on to say:
This business of saying to a woman, "You will get consideration, you will get the pension, you will get the allowance, only if you have a man,"-
-was quite rightly criticized by Mr. Knowles.
I would also remind the House that in July of 1981 I spoke to a resolution put forward by the same former Member for Winnipeg North Centre which dealt with this matter but took it one step further and really looked at the entire question of eligibility for allowances for persons who are not in the workforce, persons who are unemployed or choose to apply for pension at age 60. At that time this resolution, which was presented several times by the then Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre, concerned old age security and the guaranteed income supplement as well as the Canada Pension Plan. The recommendation was that these plans should be available at age 60. I said that they should not be available for everyone but should be for those who are not in the labour force or for those who choose, and they should have the right to choose, to retire at age 60.1 also said that they should have the assurance that they will have adequate incomes on which to survive.
In many of his remarks, the then Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre went on to say that we should also have a flexible retirement age and that persons such as himself, who at that time was over seven years beyond the age of retirement and indeed now is several years beyond that again and still sits at the Table, should not be forced to retire but should retire as a matter of choice.
The Minister isn't listening anyway. He's been very busy.

I think he is not listening. Perhaps he will read these words and ponder them later.
The Minister's own officials in the federal Department of Health and Welfare estimate that there are 80,000 men and women between the ages of 60 and 64 who are being excluded from the provisions of this Bill on the basis of marital status. In effect, Mr. Speaker, this represents the discrimination and perhaps even the sexual discrimination which is prevalent in this legislation. To quote the Government's own discussion paper on equality issues in the federal law which was raised in the House last week, I would say the following:
The question is whether marital status is an appropriate reason for choosing between equally needy people, particularly when the criteria for receipt of an allowance is need.
There should not be any reason to choose. In fact, this Bill condemns the estimated 80,000 needy people who are in the 60
Old Age Security Act
to 64-year old bracket who happen to be single to the tender mercies of their respective provincial Governments, because if they are in need they have no other alternative but to apply for welfare. We know that welfare payments are so low that many people are lining up at food banks.
I would like to refer, as did my colleague, to a task force on older women that we put in operation which presented resolutions that were accepted by the New Democratic Party in 1983. This Party, unlike the Liberal and Conservative Parties, is very proud to tell the public and the House about the type of policy which we believe is very important and which is a part of the goals that we are advocating.
As a result of our task force on older women, we presented a number of policy resolutions that apply to older women which I have advocated in this House. We advocated employment programs for women, particularly targeted to women in their middle years so that those women who have raised families and who have not had many years in the workforce would have an opportunity to pay into the Canada Pension Plan and would have equal opportunities for adequate benefits at the point of retirement. We also approved the following resolution which would provide adequate incomes for older women:
Until such time as a universal guaranteed income system is implemented-
-if ever-
-the federal government should lower the eligibility age for OAS-GIS for all unemployed people to age 60;-
Again, this is following on the resolution of Mr. Knowles.
The Old Age Pension must be raised above the poverty line with full indexing;
In view of the increasing number of unemployed and especially the number of older women living in poverty, that the NDP press the federal government to establish an action study group with a view to instituting a guaranteed annual income for older people under 65 who are unemployed-
We went on to talk of other pension reforms that were needed. I mention this because when we are looking at revisions to legislation that will affect our senior citizens and citizens in the pre-retirement ages, we should be looking at these matters in a very broad context. In many countries the pension age itself is lower than age 65. I think it is pretty regressive that we are not looking at universal pension eligibility at age 65. Until such time as we can persuade governments to look at that in a major, progressive way, we feel that the benefits for those who are covered by spousal allowances should be extended to include single people. I think this is important not only for single women but also for single men.
A recent study done in the City of Vancouver looked at unemployment in the Province of British Columbia, and I am sure the situation is the same in all provinces. This study concluded that there is a whole new group of chronic unemployed in our country which consists of older, experienced, skilled men, many of them skilled tradespeople and professionals who have now become redundant. These men are in the age group 55 to 65. I am sure many of us have encountered very tragic situations in our constituency offices. Certainly I have had many cases in my riding of construction workers, many of them immigrants from Italy, who have come to Canada, worked hard all their lives, raised families, often built their

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act
homes and who never received a cent of unemployment insurance until they reached the last year or two of their working lives. Now, those people are not only out of work and judged redundant, but they cannot qualify for retraining programs. They are on the scrap-heap. It is a terrible situation. When those people reach the age of 60 it is important that they have the option to have a minimum level of pension income until they are able to receive the full amount at age 65.
I present these points to urge the Minister not to be complacent and not to limit his planning and social policy review to the extension of the spousal allowance. We will not object to the passage of this Bill, but we must pass it with the understanding that it is very limited and that the needs of our older citizens are great and are becoming greater because of the unemployment situation which affects older people more than many of us in the middle-age group.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there questions or comments? If not, I will recognize the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Peterson).

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to thank you for recognizing me, as this is the first opportunity I have had to address the House of Commons. I would also like to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) on the contents of the Bill.
As the Member for Hamilton West, I follow in the path of two very distinguished Conservative Members. The first is the Hon. Ellen Fairclough. She has the distinction of being the First woman Cabinet Minister in Canada. In fact, last Friday she was honoured by women in Toronto. The second is the Hon. Lincoln Alexander, who was the first black Canadian to serve in the House and the first black Member of Cabinet. Both of these people contributed in their own unique way to the betterment of the City of Hamilton, this Chamber and Canada. It is certainly my hope to use their performance as a yardstick to ensure that the people of Hamilton West are properly represented.
In addition, I would like to extend my gratitude to the electorate of Hamilton West who have expressed confidence in me and in the Government.
It was 17 years ago when Lincoln Alexander, my friend and former MP from Hamilton West, rose in the House to address the Speech from the Throne. In that address he challenged the Government of the day to be socially compassionate. I agree with his remarks and I quote: "In a just society it should be the continuing responsibility of government to be constantly aware of and concerned about the degree of the quality of life which Canadians experience. If there is any disparity, no matter how little, then the Government should set itself immediately to reducing it, thereby assuring that each and every individual can live a full and productive life and become an essential part of the mainstream of Canadian life". That, coupled with the Government's commitment to a comprehensive social security system-one which responds to the changing nature and needs of our society-is encompassed in the Bill before us. The
legislation to amend the Old Age Security Act represents one of the many positive policy decisions which our Government has promised and which it will implement.
In the debates during the week prior to the Christmas recess there was a lot of heated discussion on the concept of universality of social programs. Nothing was really accomplished by the Opposition except a lot of television footage. I had the opportunity to watch those exchanges and, in the context of this Bill, I would like to offer my own thoughts on universality in our social programs.
Bill C-26 will amend the Old Age Security Act. It will amend a social program which was introduced in 1975. That social allowance, then or now, has never been universal. This Bill proposes that all low-income widowed persons aged 60 to 64 should become eligible to receive the spouse's allowance, regardless of when their spouse passed away. The Minister of National Health and Welfare stated in his news release of November 15, 1984 that income support for older Canadians-the guaranteed income supplement and the spouse's allowance-are programs which are not universal but available only to those who are in need. If these were truly universal social programs of the type that some would advocate, then all widows and widowers aged 60 to 64, regardless of their income, would receive the spouse's allowance.
If such were the case with this Bill, then the widow of our famous but fictitious $500,000 bank president who is living comfortably on investment income would also receive the benefit. Is this what some who oppose it mean when they speak about universality of social programs? I do not feel this is the logic which Canadians want their Government to apply to social programs at this time of economic restraint. Such Utopian thinking should be left to those who ponder it.
My constituents and I applaud the Minister's grab-the-bull-by-the-horns approach. It is a hands-on approach which recognizes the needs of older Canadians. It couples those needs with sound fiscal management.
Some may ask why we did not go further with this Bill and why we excluded low-income persons in the 60 to 64 age group who are single, divorced or separated from the spouse's allowance program. Estimates indicate that there are some 80,000 such individuals. In addition, there are 250,000 low-income married couples in this age category who have not received financial assistance in the form of security benefits. For the most part, assistance for any of the people who are in need will continue to be provided and administered by many of our provincial Government programs, with assistance from the federal Government, until such time as further extensions can be made responsibly. Similarly, if the spouse's allowance was provided to all low-income persons in the 60 to 64 age group, it would cost approximately $1.5 billion in the first year.
If the Liberal Opposition during their regime had exercised fiscal responsibility, the ability to provide more resources for social programs may have been possible. However, as a result of the previous Government's policies, we are prevented from
February 4, 1985

further extending the social expenditures required to facilitate all the needs of our senior Canadians. But, we cannot use the fiscal shortcomings of the previous administration as a scapegoat. Instead, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare has stated, "even in this period of economic restraint we have an obligation to those who most need our help".
With this Bill it is clear that we are fulfilling that obligation. It is an obligation which provides for widowed persons who are nearing age 65, but are not yet eligible for old age security and guaranteed income supplement benefits. It is these Canadians who are consistently identified as being the most urgently in need. In fact, it is estimated that over 60 per cent of widowed Canadians who are age 60 to 64, most of whom are women, would qualify for the proposed extension to the spouse's allowance. In December of 1985 there will be 93,000 beneficiaries collecting spouse's allowance. The proposed extension to other widowed persons aged 60 to 64 will increase the number of beneficiaries up by 85,000, with only an annual cost of $190 million in the 1985-86 fiscal year. This initiative by the Minister represented the next logical step in the provision of greater income assistance to the near elderly.
In 1979 the Conservative Government's amendments to the spouse's allowance program extended entitlements for 60 to 64-year old widowers or widows who had been receiving the spouse's allowance benefits prior to the death of the pensioner or spouse. This extension of SPA to all needy widowers or widows in this age group, as recommended by the Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform, would further remove some of the inequities which currently exist in the treatment of widows or widowers who are aged 60 to 64 under the Old Age Security Act.
This proposed amendment to Bill C-26, Mr. Speaker, results from a firm commitment made by our Party during the 1984 election campaign. In the Speech from the Throne on November 5, 1984, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) indicated that "during the coming session of Parliament we would be asked to consider legislation to extend the income-tested spouse's allowance to widows and widowers aged 60 years to 64 years regardless of the age of their spouse at death". It is indeed, Mr. Speaker, truly positive to see another campaign promise, reaffirmed in the Throne Speech, translated into legislation. This action goes a long way in restoring the faith which Canadians once had in our parliamentary system. It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that this Government is responding to the needs of all Canadians.
This is international youth year, a year of great concern for our youth, Mr. Speaker, and across Canada and throughout the world, Governments, organizations and private business should be sponsoring a wide range of awareness programs for our youth. Our Government has done so, and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) will be announcing employment incentives geared for our youth. We
Old Age Security Act
recognize the important contribution made by our young people to Canada.
In Bill C-26 the Government is showing sensitivity to the needs of our near senior Canadians, a group of Canadians who have already contributed to the wealth of our country, and nowhere is this contribution more evident than in the City of Hamilton. What is in the Bill, in my view, is necessary. It is timely and deserves the attention of the House in terms of quick passage. I can foresee no obstacles which would preempt the swift passage of this Bill through the House.

Mr. Speaker, I am also pleased that finally, after five months, the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Peterson) can speak to the Canadian people. I regret, however, that it has taken complaints on the part of the Opposition to the majority in this House and especially to those Members elected in the Hamilton area who have refrained from rising in the House until today. I expect to hear many more speeches by the Member for Hamilton West and also by the Member for Lincoln (Mrs. Martin). I know the Hon. Member is following in some very important footsteps, those of Mrs. Fairclough, among others. I was indeed delighted to be a guest last Friday at a dinner with Mrs. Fairclough. This Progressive Conservative is an example to all Canadian women, and I was very happy to be one of her guests.
He has a big pair of shoes to fill with regard to his predecessor, the former Member for Hamilton West, whom the Hon. Member did not name or perhaps forgot to name, the Hon. Stanley Hudecki, who, I think, had a reputation among all Members of this House as a member who rose above party politics and interests. He was truly an Hon. Member in every sense of the word. I just want to say, as a Member of this House, that we miss him very much.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the women of Canada, on behalf of my Party and on my own behalf, I am very pleased to support what has been said so far on the subject of the spouse's allowance. However, and I think the Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) referred to this point before, there is a small problem with respect to the present wording of the Bill. When the Bill indicates that the spouse's allowance is transferred to Canadian widows or widowers, it reflects, and I would say it does so by omission rather than by design, to recognize the economic problems facing Canadians between the ages of 60 and 64 who are either separated, divorced or single.

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act

I know, for example, Mr. Speaker, that the Government has introduced a measure which we will all support. At the same time, however, I believe we have to recognize that there is an inherent discrimination, as has been pointed out by Hon. Members on this side of the House, with respect to this particular piece of legislation. I would suggest that the Minister and his officials, in making the decision to extend the spouse's allowance to widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64-which, by the way, I think is a terrific move- should have gone that extra step and extended those same benefits to people who, for whatever reason, have chosen never to marry or who have not been as successful in their marital endeavours as others and have ended up as separated or divorced Canadians.
I know that in my own province-having had the privilege of working on the amendments to the Ontario Human Rights Code which was introduced by another Conservative Government some three years ago-that particular Government decided that within the context of the Ontario Human Rights law, there would be a non-discrimination clause on the basis of marital status. I would suggest to the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) that, prior to the implementation of this law in which there is an exclusion of separated, divorced and single Canadians, the Minister in fact investigate whether this particular proposed law is in fact in contravention of the Ontario Human Rights Code. The Human Rights Code does in fact specify that goods and services must be made available to all Canadians with no discrimination on the basis of marital status. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the current legislation in its present form is clearly discriminatory, not only toward those Canadians who have chosen never to marry but towards those who are no longer married.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, if I can speak on behalf of a number of the women in this House, that there are a number of politicians in general who, for whatever reason, have chosen to devote themselves to political life and have either not married or their marriages have not been successful. I believe there are a number of people in this House who would agree with me that the status of being a divorced or single Canadian is not one which should subject anyone to government discrimination such as will happen under the law represented by this particular Bill.
I would suggest that the original intention of the law was good, that is, to extend the current benefits which at this time are not made available to those Canadians between the ages of 60 and 64 who happen to have been widowed.
Only last weekend I had the opportunity of speaking in my constituency office with a woman who will be able to benefit through this particular Act. However, we are putting ourselves in the very difficult situation, Mr. Speaker, of actually discriminating not only on the basis of marital status-because the law will not cover separated, divorced or single Canadians-but we are also putting ourselves in the situation of discriminating against married people between the ages of 60
and 64 who naturally, notwithstanding their financial need, will not be eligible for this particular benefit as long as they remain married. I will use as an example the situation of the woman with whom I dealt most recently. She happens to be 61 years of age. Her husband was 64 when he died in the last few days only. As a result of his decease, this woman, when the Act comes into force, will be actually eligible for the benefits which would have formerly only accrued to those spouses who are married. At the same time, even though her family happens to be a family in need-neither she nor her husband were wage earners at the time of his death-if her husband had not died, he would not have been eligible for any benefits under the spouse's allowances, nor would she, until he reached the age of 65 years, which would have meant that her benefit would have been at least one year in abeyance. Therefore, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we not only have a clear case of discrimination against single, separated and divorced Canadians between the ages of 60 and 64, but we also have a possible case of discrimination against married couples, both spouses of whom happened to be between the ages of 60 and 64, who would not, under this current rather limited extension of benefits, be eligible for any assistance.
I believe, if I can read into the rationale of the Minister in introducing this legislation, he is recognizing that there is an age group in our society which under certain special circumstances needs special short-term assistance. I feel that the original introduction of the spouse's allowance as a concept, the original introduction of the guaranteed income supplement as a concept, and the original indexation of those supplements under previous Liberal Governments, were introduced because the Government recognized that, certainly in the short term, we needed to provide direct financial assistance to those individuals who were not immediately benefiting from the kind of pension reform which we are suggesting over the long term.
I certainly concur with the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) with regard to the absence of programs available to widows between the ages of 60 and 64 as well as to other unfortunate individuals who may be married and who, through no fault of their own, have lost their jobs, have not been able to compete in the technologically changing market-place, and have been left to the vagaries of the provincial welfare system. In an effort to address the discrimination issue which has been raised in this document, the Minister should consider working with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) and developing programs which will assist those Canadians who, through no fault of their own, have become disenfranchised because of the technologically changing market-place. I refer to construction workers in my own constituency.
I think it is important that we speak for all Canadians, men and women. It is certainly of interest to me as a women that this is probably the only Bill before us in the House of Commons to date in which the nomenclature used is "she" and is relating to "her", i.e., the feminine gender. I think it is implicit in the Government's approach to things that it sug-
February 4, 1985

gests that the only people who are in need of pension assistance or supplements are women. I certainly agree that it is time the Government introduced an over-all pension reform package for people across Canada and that the major beneficiaries of such a package should be the women of Canada. However, it is also about time that we recognized that we have a responsibility to all Canadian women and men between the ages of 60 and 64. We must guarantee them some kind of an economic security.

Mr. Speaker, in its present form, the Bill is clearly discriminatory. It not only discriminates against people who are single or were never married or whose marriage failed, it also discriminates against those who are married today to a woman or a man between sixty and sixty-four years old. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has taken a small step, but I think he should now take a bigger one. If he really intends to tackle this issue courageously, he should immediately bring before the House a complete package of changes to our pension system to help those who are in need, men and women, men between 60 and 64 and women between 60 and 64, whether they are single, widowed or still married.
We know there are couples who need help. The husband or wife, for some reason, and I will give you another example... Last week, in my riding, I met a family where the husband who had worked for more than twenty years for a company called Canron, was fired as of February 1 because the company closed down. His wife worked for Arrow Shirts for fourteen years, and last year in November she was laid off because of lack of work in the textile industry and because this Government had failed to take certain measures in this area. It means that two people between the ages of sixty and sixty-four who have worked all their lives are now being fired by their employers within three months of each other. It will be almost impossible for them to find work.
To help these families it is not enough to bring in a small package of reforms that apply only to widows and widowers. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) should set up a clear-cut plan to reform the pension system, which I think would have the support of all Canadians, and especially Members on this side of the House.

We need more than simply very small reform in pension benefits for a very restricted group of Canadians. We need an over-all pension and re-employment strategy involving the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) with respect to the ILAP designations, which have been helpful in certain sectors. The Minister of Employment and Immigration must also be involved. A designation under ILAP could assist many of the workers at Consolidated Bathurst in my own community who are facing financial ruin and bankruptcy and will be reduced to welfare
Old Age Security Act
roles. The majority of them had combined years of service of over 25 years when the company chose to close its doors.
We need more than the measures which are being introduced. We need an over-all strategy. In expressing his concern for older Canadians, the Minister of National Health and Welfare should act with the Minister of Employment and Immigration to develop programs which will assist our seniors financially and help them re-integrate into the workplace when that is possible.
The only thing that many older Canadians have been offered by the current Government is a threat that if they remain on unemployment insurance benefits for too long one of Flora's private police force will ensure that they are removed from them. In the context of the employment programs that are going to be launched by the Government, it behooves all of us to remember those Canadians who have been disenfranchised by the technological age and have found themselves on the street when companies have closed their doors.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: What is the relevance of this?

The Minister of National Health and Welfare may find it terribly irrelevant that I am talking about older workers who have lost their jobs. The Minister will be aware that we must ensure that widows as well as divorced and single people are receiving assistance from the Government when they need it most. We must also ensure that those workers between the ages of 60 and 64 who happen, through no fault of their own, to be married, can receive some assistance from the Government. The Minister is suggesting that my concern for workers between the ages of 60 and 64 who happen to be married are not covered under the legislation. It is a concern, and that is the relevance of my remarks to this particular Bill.
Excluding married couples, separated, divorced and single people between the ages of 60 and 64 suggests that the Government has no programs to assist them and is directing its efforts only toward one rather small segment of the demographic population between the ages of 60 and 64. No one would argue that the Government should be ignoring the small, albeit deserving, group of widows and widowers. At the same time the Minister must work with the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Employment and Immigration to ensure that older workers who have been contributing for 20 or 30 years and, through no fault of their own, find themselves out on the street, will receive an indication from the Government as to the action it is prepared to take. Rather than doing away with the general training incentives and cutting back on the amount of government based job creation through Canada Works, the Government must come forth with innovative programs. These programs should be targeted not only to young people who need job opportunities but also to the older workers. Most specifically, they should be directed to the target group that is being addressed in this legislation.

Members from all sides of the House who have had a chance to meet with those workers in their constituency on a daily or weekly basis will know that there is nothing more heart-rending than to meet a grown man in tears because he has lost a job after 30 years and is on the street with nowhere to go.
I ask the Minister to work with his colleagues to make sure that there are programs to assist those workers. The Government cannot simply turn its back on those workers between the ages of 60 and 64 who may not come under the category being addressed by this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare says that this has nothing to do with the Bill. It has quite a lot to do with the Bill, for had he had an opportunity to meet with those workers aged 60 to 64 who have lost their jobs, who have been laid off as a result of plant closures, he would know indeed that those workers, widows and widowers alike, need assistance under the programs, they need from this Government very specific help measures such as they do not have at this time.
Well, Mr. Speaker, perhaps you might urge the Minister to join forces with all interested parties in the various departments-the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of Labour, for instance-with a view to implementing a genuine economic policy for all needy Canadians without jobs between ages 60 and 64. What we do not need is a Bill which discriminates against unmarried people, those who are divorced or separated, or those who are still married and whose spouses are under 65. Give us that kind of policy and you will have our full support, because we in the Liberal Party realize that the people most in need in our society right now are those people between 60 and 64 who have been laid off through no fault of their own and who are without hope, who have not been promised anything, or who have had lots of promises but no action on the part of this Government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That explains a lot of things.

Members may recall that last week, when the Minister rose, he was pointing out how he went home and read over the reports and came to the conclusion that what he was doing was right. I went back and read over Hansard and came to the conclusion that, to the extent that the Minister, the Ministry and the Government are doing anything at all in this regard, what they are doing is right. In fact, not only is it
Old Age Security Act
right, it is consistent with what our Party has been suggesting the Minister ought to do for many years. In fact, as I was saying, as reported on page 16597 of Hansard, when the Liberal Party was in government, my good friend and former colleague, the previous Member for Winnipeg North Centre, the Hon. Stanley Knowles, now frequently seated at the table, asked the then Minister of Health and Welfare, the Hon. Monique Begin, the following:
My question this afternoon relates to my concern about the unfairness of the plan respecting old age pensions under which certain women-there are some men but it is mostly women-between the ages of 60 and 65 can get a pension provided they are married to someone who is 65 or over. However, persons between the ages of 60 and 65 who are single, whose husbands died before that age, are not allowed any such pension. Will the Minister seriously consider a plan to change that, so that persons between the ages of 60 and 65 who are in need will get that kind of pension?
The Member went on to explain some other regrets. This was his first day back in the House, Mr. Speaker, you may recall, after he had suffered that rather serious illness from which be made a remarkable and miraculous recovery.
When I started, I wanted to congratulate the Minister for having recognized the need, and I do. I understand that for those who will receive this, it will be a godsend. They will be delighted to have it, and have it they must. I say to the Minister though that he has not quite gone far enough. The cost of going the extra distance is difficult to determine, I must say, but nevertheless it is a cost that I believe ought to be borne.
It is unnecessary, I suggest to the Minister, to restrict this payment to those individuals who have been married. The former Member for Winnipeg-North Centre, Mr. Knowles, made reference to that. In his question, in 1982, he indicated his concern for those between the ages of 60 and 65, who were single and who found themselves unable to continue to work for a number of economic or, for that matter, health reasons and who found themselves without any regular adequate income.
The Minister frequently speaks about compassion. I know him well enough to know that he speaks with conviction. He speaks with compassion about compassion. I do not in any way question him, and I think this would be an opportunity for him to display that compassion beyond what the Government may well have identified it wants to do in the meantime and to take into account the submissions of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young). He has suggested that perhaps this would be the time to enlarge the scope and to look at ways of taking into account the needs of those who were never married but who nevertheless are between the ages of 60 and 65-I want to talk about other people in a moment-and who are frankly in very difficult Financial straits at this point in the history of Canada.
I must be honest and admit that I do not have an economic analysis of it-I do not know whether the Minister has or not and if he does, I would be interested to hear it-nor do I have any kind of accounting that would show me clearly and in

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act
accurate terms exactly what the cost would be to extend this level of benefit to other than simply the spouses of those who have been in receipt of the old age pension. I do want to suggest to the Minister that, whatever the cost, I do not think it is impossible for us to find a way to fund it. I do not think for one moment it is impossible for us to reallocate funding from other less worthy causes. I do not think it is impossible for us to look into ways of making this available.
It strikes me that an allowance based on need-which this allowance is I think we all agree-that has as its primary criterion that one has to have been married is unfair. It is unfair, Mr. Speaker. If an allowance is based on need, it ought to be paid to those who are in need on the same basis. If you are in need, you are in need and whether you were or were not married does not alter the fact that you are in need. If your circumstances are the same in terms of your financial capacities, then quite clearly you should be treated in the same way by your Government.
I think the distance that the Minister has gone is fine, but I seriously urge the Minister to go the other short distance and attempt to find a way to accommodate the question to which my colleague who formerly represented Winnipeg North Centre, my colleague from Beaches, and probably my colleague who now represents the riding of Winnipeg North Centre would want him to give some consideration.
I know the Minister himself is aware of the speeches made in the House of Commons by his colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), as recently as May 10, 1984. She made speeches on other days going back to June and February, 1984. There were statements made by another colleague on those occasions with regard to the problems of people in Canada who, because of the economic conditions that now exist, and which did not exist in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, are unable to find employment. They have not yet attained what we consider to be the normal retirement age and, as a result of that, they are unable to continue to hold on to what they accumulated throughout their lifetime as a result of hard work.
I do not doubt, when the Minister goes back to Provencher, that he meets in his constituency office every weekend or at the church on Sunday mornings with citizens who are in their middle fifties, maybe in their late fifties, who have worked hard all of their lives and who have been employed perhaps in many instances by the only major employer in the area. Perhaps that major employer has ceased to operate for any number of reasons, and if he has not ceased to operate, at least is operating at a dramatically reduced level. I am confident that there are people who have brought to the Minister's attention the terrible situation in which they have found themselves.
On the weekend in Hamilton-I am sure it is the same in every constituency, I do not doubt that for a moment and no doubt my colleague, the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Peterson), meets the same kind of people I do-I had an opportunity to discuss with a family its particular difficulty. Here was a man and his wife who over the many years raised a
family, had worked at one of the plants in Hamilton and worked there for the better part of 30 years, not quite, but almost. He had an excellent work record but suddenly discovered that the plant in terms of its management was redundant. This plant no longer manufactured a product that was saleable in the consumer market-place. It was not his fault. Every day he went in and he made the product he was asked to make. He made it to the best of his ability, and the company sold it. Gradually, with the passage of time and the introduction of new technology, it became unnecessary for that product to be made. This man, it could be said as an aside-and I am not sure if one can make an aside to something one says oneself-was the victim of two things, neither of them of his own making. He was a victim of a changing market condition and of a rapidly changing economic climate. He may well have been the victim of bad decision-making on the part of the management of the company, which ought to have been able, with proper planning, to alter the manufacturing process, seek out additional markets and manufacture new products. Unfortunately, that did not happen.
Here he is at age 56. He has been to many employers. I have personally sent him to a number of people who I thought might give him a job, but he cannot find one in the Hamilton area, he travelled to Toronto, Kitchener and down to St. Catharines, but there were no jobs. He came to the conclusion somewhat reluctantly that his age is working against him. Although we all know that we cannot discriminate because of age, there are hints that that sort of thing happens. It is not unreasonable to think that at age 56 maybe he is being overlooked just because of his age. He offered to take anything. He cannot find anything. He ran out of unemployment insurance benefits and therefore has no income of his own. His wife works but only part time because she cannot find a job. They have to pay what is left on the mortgage which they assumed 20 years ago. It is not a great deal, but nevertheless it is there. They cannot make their payments. What do we do for a man like this? What do we say to someone like this? He is representative of a host of people.
The Minister brought forward this particular amendment to the Old Age Security Act. Again I say to him in all fairness and honesty that I applaud the initiative. However, it does not really address today's problems. It addresses a part of today's problems, a very small part, but it obviously does not address the much larger, if not more important, problem confronting many workers in the 55 to 60 age group. We have reached the point where we in the House of Commons as Members of Parliament have an obligation to look seriously at the plight of those people about whom I am talking today in a representative sense. We have an obligation to find the ways necessary for them to re-enter the workforce. The Government would love it to happen, but it is realistic and recognizes that with tens if not hundreds of thousands of people in the age bracket of 20 to 30 also looking for work, the chance of our being able to entice employers to hire those in their later fifties and early sixties is somewhat difficult. Also, we would be put in the
February 4, 1985

position of playing off one age group against another. I find that offensive, to say the least. We have reached the point where this administration, if it wants to make a mark on Canadian history politically, must move to reform basic pension plans.
This legislation will not do it. Tinkering will not be enough. There is nothing as devastating as to have worked all your life and to reach the point where you are finally looking ahead seven, eight or nine years to retirement, only to discover that not only do you not have a job, not only do you not have an income of some reasonable proportion, but during the period of time you had anticipated you would be working you are not contributing to a pension plan. This reduces pensionable income and therefore reduces the income received when you reach what is generally accepted as the pension age. You are caught in a catch-22 situation. On the one hand, you have no income while you are supposed to be working because you cannot find work and you are losing the assets you accumulated through your labour. On the other hand, because you do not have that income you are detrimentally affecting, if not eliminating, the potential pension income you would have had, had you been able to work to the normal retirement age.
It is unacceptable that we as a Parliament are not dealing with that issue right now. I know the Minister feels as strongly as I do about it. This has to become one of the highest priorities of Parliament. We cannot afford to gloss it over, neither can we afford to be overly lavish in our praise of the small change. We are thankful for the small change. Those who will receive it will be grateful for it and it is right that they should get it, but it is insignificant when viewed over and against the need.
I want simply to say to the Minister that whatever else the Government believes it has on its agenda, we have to deal with this matter. We must deal with it. We cannot put if off. There is no way back for those individuals. With every passing month, with every passing year, the dilemma confronting them becomes even more enormous and the hardship more unacceptable. We cannot apologize to them eight years from now and say, "We really wish we could have done something for you; unfortunately it was just not possible". That will be too late for them. Therefore, it is necessary that we agree together in the House that we will find the time to deal as expeditiously as possible with the dilemma confronting those particular people about whom I speak today.
If the Minister will commit himself to bringing forward legislation in this regard during this session of this Parliament, I will commit this Party to making sure that we put forth every single effort we can to guarantee the success of the legislation. I ask him to recognize that delay compounds the hardship. We simply cannot have delay on this matter.
