Mr. Speaker, thank you very much for recognizing me. I started a diet this morning and I thought for a minute that I was having excellent success and would not be recognized.
This is the first time I have risen in the House to speak formally in a debate. I would ask for your patience for a few moments so that I might acknowledge and congratulate you on your appointment as Acting Speaker. I know you will do a great job, as you have done to this point. Also I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). This is the first opportunity I have had to do so. I know he will do an excellent job. I had the opportunity of working with him when I was a Minister in the provincial Government. I know how dedicated he is to his position of responsibility and his desire to do well for the Canadian public.
I also take this opportunity to thank my constituents for showing me that they had faith in my ability to be their Member. I will try to live up to their expectations. Particularly I thank all those people who worked for me during my campaign.
Winnipeg-St. James is a relatively new riding. It was assembled in 1979 with the redistribution and was represented by a friend of mine, Mr. Robert Lane, a Progressive Conservative.

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act
It was then held by the present Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper). For some reason he decided to move to the constituency formerly held by the Hon. Stanley Knowles. Whatever were the reasons that made him decide this, it seems to have worked out well for both him and me.
Winnipeg-St. James is an urban riding. The Winnipeg International Airport is almost in the centre of my riding. As the Member of Parliament for Winnipeg-St. James, I cannot guarantee that I will welcome you every time you arrive there, even though that may be the custom. That gives a general idea of the location of our riding.
The riding is a good cross-section of Manitoba. Citizens of over 20 ethnic backgrounds form an integral part of the social fabric of Manitoba. Like most Manitobans, they are very hard working citizens. Some are long-time residents, some are immigrants, and some are new Canadian citizens. We have a good cross-section of the various citizens in our province in my riding.
We have blue collar workers, executives and free entrepreneurs, so we have a cross-section of the business community as well. Without getting you too excited, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that it is the home base of the Grey Cup champions for 1984, the Winnipeg Blue Bombers. I tried to congratulate them under Standing Order 21, and I almost got it through. At this time I would like to congratulate the Winnipeg Blue Bombers, the reigning Grey Cup champions.
Hear, hear!

I did not want to say that the Speaker used to be an Edmonton Eskimo. I am proud and privileged to represent Winnipeg-St. James. Having made those few comments, I would now like to speak to the Bill.
As a former Minister of Community Services in the Province of Manitoba, I had day-to-day contact with the very problem that this Bill will help to alleviate. I know the sincerity and commitment of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). I applaud him for the first step he has taken in alleviating the problem that exists for the 60 to 64 years olds in the low income bracket. I support his approach to consultation with the- public and the provinces. The Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) commented on the former Liberal Government consulting with the provinces and being leader in the consultation field. That was not the case when I was Minister of Community Services. If being called to a meeting, sitting at a table and having the federal Minister say what the Government was going to do is consultation, I will not agree. I know the present Health Minister will not follow that approach.
The objective of this Bill is to provide assistance to low income widowed persons in the 60 to 64 year age group who meet the same 10 year residence rule as other spouse's allowance recipients without regard to the age at which the spouse died. As a result of this reform in the present law, about
85,000	widowers and widows aged 60 to 64 will qualify. There
is a definite need for this. I understand that when this Bill is passed and the program comes into effect in September, about 61 per cent of the entire widowed population in that age group will qualify. This clearly indicates that there is a need in this area and we will be alleviating part of that need.
The maximum benefit will be $536.26 per month and will be income tested. This reform will remove the inequities which currently exist in the treatment of low income widowed persons. It represents the next logical step in the provision of greater income assistance for the needy elderly. The proposal to extend the spouse's allowance was a firm commitment of our Party during the election. It was a promise in the Throne Speech. I am happy we are meeting that commitment. I congratulate the Minister on bringing forward the legislation at this time.
I wish to comment briefly on the general background of the development of pensions. I think it comes into play with what the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) talked about. It has been accepted in the past and is at present that the federal Government has the prime responsibility for pensions such as the old age security, the guaranteed income supplement and the Canada Pension Plan. The reason is primarily the immense cost to fund these types of programs. The provincial Governments have taken on the share of responsibilities with the federal Government on other social services such as income security programs, welfare and rehabilitation. I am confident the Minister will look into these because there are now areas of responsibility being split and, in some cases, being duplicated.
What is the economic impact of our spouse's allowance program? I understand that in December, 1985 there will be some 93,681 recipients of the spouse's allowance with program costs in the area of $11.5 billion. Therefore, it has a big economic impact on the budget of the Government of Canada. The proposed extension to all widows and widowers will be in the order of some $350 million when the program is in the full year of operation. It has a fairly heavy economic impact on the Government's expenditures.
What are the long-term objectives for the low income single individual? We in this House would like to see the step taken whereby any single person between the ages of 60 and 64 and is needy will qualify. I am confident that the Minister will work to that end. It amplifies the problem which the Government faces. The Minister indicated many times in this House that we need economic growth in order to provide these extended services which all Members would like to see. It stresses the importance of our program of regaining confidence in this country by both investors and citizens so that we as private entrepreneurs can reinvest in creating jobs and creating the revenue for financing these programs.
We are all concerned about those who are not covered by this Bill. The low income person between the ages of 60 and 64 who may be single or divorced, and there are 80,000 such individuals, will continue to have assistance provided through provincial programs. I want to mention this because the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain hit on a fact of which many
February 4, 1985

of us might not be aware, that is, that there are provincial programs. They vary from province to province. They look after some of the problems he cited. Given the current economic situation, it would be difficult to meet the needs of all persons in this age category through federal benefits. If the spouse's allowance were provided to all low income persons, we would be looking at something in the order of $1.5 billion. Again, that is more money from the taxpayer.
I would like to remind Members of the House that governments do not have money. Governments spend taxpayers' money. That was taught to me approximately 18 years ago when I was first elected to the City of St. James Council. Do you know who taught me that, Mr. Speaker? It was a Liberal, and I might say he was a very fine and hard-working man by the name of Reg Wightman.
Must be dead now.

Yes, unfortunately he is.
The former Liberal Government did not recognize that fact. What did it do? It spent and spent and spent, and then it spent again. Then it borrowed and borrowed and borrowed some more until it had borrowed to the tune of $190 billion. I believe that governments must have a conscience. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if it is right to borrow money continually on behalf of our youth and our future taxpayers, committing them as citizens of this country to pay back these debts without even consulting with them. That is what is happening when we have a deficit.
I might remind the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) who spoke about discrimination that having no regard for future taxpayers by spending wildly is, I suggest, a form of discrimination against the future taxpayers of Canada including the women of Canada. If we create such large debts that interest expenditures approach 75 per cent of what we borrow, then we will have to restrict our social programs, and that will affect the very women to whom the Hon. Member for Hamilton East was referring.
I think it is wrong to borrow money continually on behalf of future taxpayers. Our Government is committed to reducing that deficit with which we are now faced, and that is one of the reasons why we cannot afford to take that one extra step which all of us would like to take at this time to help the needy in the age group of 60 to 64. In my estimation, the taxpayers cannot afford that $1.5 billion per year. Some day after our economy keeps growing and after the Government puts its own House in order, we will be able to afford that.
Because of the earlier comments of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain, I would like to comment on some of the provincial programs that are available in Manitoba for the needy, programs which are federally cost shared through the Canada Assistance Plan. I believe this amounts to somewhere in the order of $3.9 billion in total across Canada. As Minister of Community Services for Manitoba, I was part of a Progressive Conservative Government which instituted the new pro-
Old Age Security Act
grams and extended existing programs to deal partially with the needy aged 60 to 64. I say that we dealt partially with those needy people. One of the major steps that the Sterling Lyon Government of Manitoba took was to lower the qualification age from 65 to 55. We found that there is a need felt not only by those of the age group of 60 to 65 but also by those of the age group of 55 to 60. Furthermore, an individual could qualify for some of these programs if at least 50 per cent of his or her income came from a pension. Those were the basic criteria we established.
The particular age group to which we are referring right now is unique. I do not believe that the problems this age group faces now will exist in 20 years because of the fact that we are entering a stage in life in which both the husband and wife work and are paying toward pensions. We may have to adjust some of these programs down the road to accommodate that.
To give you an idea of some of the programs that we developed, Mr. Speaker, the Manitoba supplement for pensioners which was already in existence that paralleled the guaranteed income supplement was doubled. We were a very progressive Conservative Government. We doubled the amount of money the citizens received and lowered the qualifying age to 55. We also developed what we called a shelter allowance for elderly renters, and this allowed someone who was over the age of 55 to qualify for up to $1,448 per year in allowance toward rent if he or she fell within the income bracket about which we are speaking. In addition to that, we provided an additional rebate on education tax for homeowners or renters. We expanded that so that if homeowners or renters fell into a certain income bracket, they would receive an additional rebate on their education tax. As we all know as Members of Parliament, there is as well what is called the income security through the social allowance, which is always the last resort and is very demeaning to the individual who must receive that allowance. I hope that some day that allowance will not be required by people aged 60 to 64.
I hope that I will have an opportunity to speak on a future Bill which will provide an allowance for single needy citizens aged 60 to 64. I am confident that I will, for the more our economy grows, the greater is the probability.

The comment I would like to make is that I do not think there is anyone who does not want to do everything possible for everyone they can help. However, the problem in this country is productivity. We have been borrowing ourselves into debt.

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act
We owe $200 billion. Until we are able to start reducing our deficit and increasing our productivity, there is a real danger of even holding on to the social programs we have today.
When speaking to people in my riding who need help, I find that their biggest fear is that governments will go overboard and eventually leave them with nothing. If we go too far, we finally find that we do not have anything because we do not have the productivity to cover anything. I would urge all Canadians to increase productivity at the fastest possible rate. Let us get our entrepreneurs investing so we will have jobs. When we do that, we will get closer and closer to being in a position in which we can fill that gap and look after all the people who need help. It is the productivity that will determine it in the final run.
I would like to commend the Hon. Member for touching upon these points. Certainly there are many programs across the nation, but there are very few if any programs designed for single women between the ages of 55 and 65 and there are some real needs there. Let us increase our productivity so that we can look after these needy cases. That and not borrowing will be the answer.
Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say that I agree with the comments made by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) and I thank him for asking the question.

Mr. Speaker, I think that many congratulations have been extended today and when I heard what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker) said about you, I thought for a moment that you would leave the chair but you decided with humility not to do so.
I wish the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) could stay and listen to what Hon. Members have to say about Bill C-26 which I consider quite important. I would have liked to congratulate him and I also wanted him to attend-

speechtext: Order. The Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault) on a point of order.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that the Hon. Member is referring to the attendance of the minister in this House. Those remarks are contrary to Standing Orders and practices of this House.

speechtext: I regret but this is not a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I said before that I was sorry not to see the Minister, who has now left the House-probably to attend to certain duties at his department-because I would have liked him to hear what I have to propose or say to him at the end of my speech. I know the Minister is a very dedicated person. I have known him for quite some time, and I am sure he is the right man in the right job, and as I said earlier, I want to congratulate him on presenting a bill, Bill C-26, which, I think, complements the Old Age Security Act.
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to repeat what has already been said: how many people are involved-about 85,000; that the Bill mainly affects widows and widowers; and that it neglects a segment of the population that is in similar circumstances, namely, 80,000 people who are single, divorced or separated. It is an excellent piece of legislation, one in a long line of old age security programs established by the previous Government, and it clearly shows the evolution that is taking place with respect to the old age security system.
This has been happening since 1975. The first step was to give the spouse who had not yet reached the age of sixty-five and was married to a pensioner of sixty-five the right to receive a spouse's allowance, provided certain conditions were met. Around 1979, another amendment was added to deal with the fact that if the pensioner died, the surviving spouse who had not yet reached the age of sixty-five was automatically eliminated from the program. That, as I said earlier, was another step in the evolution of our social security legislation.
However, 80,000 Canadians are being left out. I suppose it is understandable that for budgetary reasons and other considerations, this Bill is not as complete as we would have hoped. However, it is absolutely essential that we review the entire question of old age security-I would suggest the words "golden age" instead of old age. We must find a mechanism to provide all Canadians who are in need and who have reached the age of sixty some kind of guaranteed income, which would automatically eliminate the Canada Pension Plan, the Old Age Security Pension and any other allowances involved, such as income security, for people who have reached the age of sixty.
Before we reach that goal of course, there are many ways of trying to improve the existing system. In Quebec for instance, the Regie des rentes has amended its regulations so that people aged 60 years and over who are no longer active on the labour market can draw a pension at age 60 subject to a penalty.
I do not know whether the Minister of National Health and Welfare has done this, but the former Minister, Miss Begin, was due to meet with her provincial counterparts in June last, to discuss the important issue of amendments to the Canadian Pension Plan along the lines developed by the Quebec Regie des rentes, to allow taxpayers to retire at age 60 and draw benefits from the Canada Pension Plan, provided they are no longer on the labour market, and subject to a certain penalty. In so doing, we would have put many more people to work. We could also have satisfied the needs of those who are in need, as
February 4, 1985

was mentioned earlier, but have no program to help them adequately. I am not suggesting that this would have solved all the problems, but it could at least have solved some of them and it could have given people something to help them out of misery, at least temporarily.
However, this has not been done. I wonder why. But I think we should think very seriously about amending the Canada Pension Plan, along the lines developed by the Province of Quebec last Summer.
This is causing exceptional and extraordinary hardship to people especially to those hundreds of thousands of civil servants who have worked all their lives in the Province of Quebec and now live in Ontario, and to those in Quebec who have worked all their lives in Ontario, as this does happen in the Hull-Ottawa area where there are 100,000 federal civil servants. Actually a civil servant from Quebec who has worked all his life in Ontario, cannot retire at age 60, while his Ontario counterpart who has worked in Quebec all his life can retire at 60.
There is inequity in my view, something we should change. Because when the Canada Pension Plan was established and the Province of Quebec decided they would have their own plan, the agreement was that both plans would work along the same lines, which means that whenever the Province of Quebec or Canada would amend their respective pension plan legislation, there should have been, if there were not in fact, consultations to avoid the current inequities. I suggest the Minister of National Health and Welfare would be well-advised to very seriously consider what I just listed in the way of possible changes as between the Quebec Regie des rentes and the Canada Pension Plan.
In my view, as it has been so often repeated in this House, this is a complementary bill, a very good bill.
I hope that we shall go much farther, not only in providing assistance, but also in giving those who have contributed so much to Canada some security in their old age which is itself unfortunately a natural handicap whose consequences we must all endure as we grow older. In addition, available income is much lower for this group of Canadians.
It is therefore imperative that we find the means to provide a guaranteed income for needy people who have reached a certain age, such as 60. I can also tell the House that, according to actuarial projections, we should consider this problem as soon as possible since the birth rate in Canada seems far from what we might describe as "healthy", and if the present trend continues, there will be a reversal in the normal pyramid of ages with many young people at the bottom and fewer older people at the top in view of the decrease in the number of young people. There will eventually be a great number of older people or of people about to reach the age of 60, which will represent an enormous danger for the Canadian
Old Age Security Act
society, the Treasury and Government budgets, whatever the party in power.
When we say that the provincial Governments have excellent bridging programs, that is programs to provide support for people before they reach the age of 60 or 65, we should remember that the federal Government is the one to foot the bill since 50 per cent of the costs of all social security programs in Canada are paid by federal taxes, by transfer payments to the provinces so they will be able to pay for their own social programs.
This is what I wanted to say, Mr. Speaker. I could go on much longer but everything has already been said and I do not want to be repetitive. I simply want to point out to the House that eligibility for pensions plans in Canada should be lowered, so that a contributor can decide when he reaches 60 and no longer works that he will receive his pension subject to a few penalties, which I have already explained. This would provide employment for many more people and meet the needs of a forgotten group of citizens with virtually no income, and it would allow these people to live their remaining years with relatively few problems.
Mr. Speaker, this is what I wanted to say, and once more, I want to thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare for having thought of those who unfortunately cannot protect themselves or see to their own needs. I hope that he will continue in this spirit and that he will introduce in the near, and even the very near future, a bill which will cover old age security benefits and guaranteed income supplements for the people who have been forgotten in this bill, namely those who are single, divorced or separated and who number 80,000 in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to participate in this debate, even if I can only begin my comments today.
It will be the best five minutes the House has had today.

I appreciate the complimentary comment made by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith).
I would like to begin my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by paying tribute to the former Member for Winnipeg North Centre, the Hon. Stanley Knowles. I would also like to pay tribute to his predecessor, J. S. Woodsworth, and to the social and political movement in this country of which I am a part, the CCF and the NDP. I begin that way, Mr. Speaker, because both Mr. Knowles and Mr. Woodsworth and the Parties of which they were a part had a very significant impact on pensions in this country. Without the contribution of these individuals and

February 4, 1985
Old Age Security Act
without the political movement of which they were a part, we would not have the pensions we do today.
In 1926 the old age pension was first enacted, and it was only enacted because of pressure from J. S. Woodsworth, who was the first Leader of the CCF. He was able to bring pressure to bear on the Government of the day because it was in a minority situation. Because of the dedication of this man and of the people who supported him, and because of the vulnerability of the Government of the day, pensions were first introduced in this country. Obviously, not only members of the CCF Party were involved, but people in the labour movement and people of social concern right across the country were pushing for this innovation.
In 1966, again facing a minority Government, the New Democratic Party was able to pressure the Government to establish the Canada Pension Plan. I think it is only fitting that I take this brief opportunity to acknowledge the work of my predecessor, the Hon. Stanley Knowles, in this important area. We are fortunate to have him here in the House today during this debate on pensions. He serves as a reminder that the fight for adequate pensions in this country has been going on for a long time. Obviously, we have much more work to do in this area. We are really building today on the shoulders of those who did the work before us.
In 1973, Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party, and Mr. Knowles, were once again able to force a minority Government to take further action in the area of pensions and establish the full indexing of the Canada Pension Plan. So I wanted to begin my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by paying tribute to the work of Mr. Knowles, who is with us today, and to Mr. Woodsworth before him and to the socialist movement of which I am a part, the New Democratic Party which arose from the CCF.
We in this Party are prepared to support the legislation which is before us because it does extend additional benefits to some 85,000 Canadians who are in need of those benefits. These beneficiaries are elderly women between the ages of 60 and 64 who are spouses of people who are eligible for the pension. This legislation which is before the House will therefore receive our support.
Hon. members of my Party who have already spoken in this debate have pointed out that not only those who are married and the elderly need additional benefits. There is also a group of people who are single, who have never married, who also need the extension of pension benefits. We are, therefore, bringing to the attention of this Government the need of these people and pointing out that simply to deal with the needs of those who are married and to forget the needs of those who are single throughout their adult lives is discriminatory.

That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Farm Credit Act in order to provide for a guarantee to any person that takes or holds a mortgage on farm property.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my motion before the House this afternoon in Private Members' Hour was before the House in the form of a Bill in the last Parliament. It simply provides for an amendment to the Farm Credit Act to enable the Corporation to guarantee mortgages. This cannot be put forward in the form of a Bill in the House by a Private Member because it has financial implications. However, I hope that the Government will be in favour of having this matter referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture. I believe the idea would be very beneficial. If we cannot pass it as an amendment to the Farm Credit Act, at least it could be reviewed by the Standing Committee on Agriculture. If it was found to be acceptable there, there would be a positive report to the House to make this amendment to the Farm Credit Act.
If this motion were to be adopted by the Government, it would have two very important applications to the Act. It would enable a farmer who is retiring and selling his farm to his son or a neighbour's son to take back a mortgage. After proper appraisal of the property, the Farm Credit Corporation would be able to guarantee that property. There could perhaps be provisions that if the farmer selling the property passes away the guarantee would be implemented.
The greatest problem in agriculture today is the financial crisis. It is due to many things. Clearly, a simple amendment to the Farm Credit Act cannot solve all of those problems. During the past 10 years, farm commodity prices have stayed approximately the same or gone down a little bit. Input costs have continued to rise. Farm interest rates went up very high and then dropped down to some extent.
The most serious aspect is that farm land values have dropped by up to 25 per cent and in some cases up to 50 per cent during the last two or three years. The agricultural community, including the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Canadian Cattlemen's Association and the National Farmers' Union, is asking for a system of agricultural financing in the country with interest rates far below the regular
February 4, 1985

commercial rates. Many farmers who are retiring would be willing to sell their farms and take back a mortgage at lower interest rates of perhaps 8 per cent or 9 per cent if they had a loan guarantee by the Farm Credit Corporation. This would achieve two purposes. Retiring farmers often have difficulty finding someone with the capital or long-term debt money to purchase the farm. Young farmers often have difficulty getting a mortgage at reasonable interest rates.
This proposal of providing a loan guarantee would be very beneficial to our agriculture community. It would be of assistance to young farmers starting out looking for relatively low interest rates and to retiring farmers. The retiring farmer knows that if he takes back a mortgage and provides a reduction in the interest rate the mortgage will be guaranteed. I think that is a very important aspect. The crisis of dropping land values would be helped by this situation because longterm money would be available.
The second aspect of this motion is with regard to the emergency situation which we face in our country today. Land values have dropped by 25 per cent or 30 per cent. Farmers who were in a strong equity position have suddenly lost their equity position. Last Thursday members of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture had consultations with Members of Parliament from Ontario. One of the members spoke about his hog operation in northern Ontario. He purchased a farm for $320,000 about 10 years ago. He took out a $240,000 mortgage with the Farm Credit Corporation. The hog operation was appraised last year at $165,000. In other words, he had lost half of his equity. The Government must take some action to resolve this problem. Simple foreclosures just drive down land values.
The United States government has established a set aside program under its farmers' home administration program. It has some 273,000 loans. It has lent about $25 million or $27 million. On approximately September 18 it notified farmers that it was establishing a farmers' loan set aside program whereby it would set aside one-quarter of their mortgage for a period of up to five years, provided that that would put their farming operation in a positive cash flow situation with a 10 per cent margin. I believe that in the long run that type of program will save a lot more farms than the Minister will with his little three point program which will allow some farmers to reduce their mortgage interest rate from 14 per cent to 12.75 per cent. They can appeal a decision by the Farm Credit Corporation if it is going to foreclose. In a number of counties in southwestern Ontario there is a review board consisting of an agriculture representative, an FCC representative and others from the community. Such a consultation and appeal procedure is of some benefit because it gets the creditors together. However, there is no legislative authority to set aside a portion of the loan.
With respect to the U.S. system, besides the set aside program for the direct farmers' home administration loan, there is a program whereby other lending institutions such as
Farm Credit Act
banks, credit unions and production co-ops will forgive a portion of the debt to at least 10 per cent. The farmers' home administration will provide a loan guarantee of 90 per cent of the balance of the mortgage.
My motion would provide that kind of loan guarantee. This type of program has been adopted in the United Sates and, I understand they have already set aside some $3,000 in loans under the farmers home administration.
Those are the two applications that I see for this provision which I am suggesting for the Farm Credit Corporation Act. We would then be able to provide that kind of loan guarantee, and I think it would help young farmers in financial difficulty as well as retiring farmers who want to give a favourable interest rate to young farmers who are just starting out. They would also have their position protected by the guarantee, and the Farm Credit Corporation would be protected also because it would do a proper appraisal, they would have a loan guarantee, and I am sure there would be supervision over the loan to ensure that the obligations were met.
The more urgent problem is that of the short-term set aside program. I believe the Minister will act in the near future to establish a program in this regard. I do not say that because I am in the Opposition and do not have the responsibility of a government Member, but because I believe that it is the right step to take. If one examines farm bankruptcies or foreclosures in Canada, one finds that the average loss to the Farm Credit Corporation is $80,000 to $90,000. If the Farm Credit Corporation were to set aside a portion of the loan for a period of four or five years, as has been done in the United States, surely the interest on that portion of the loan set aside will not be the $80,000 or $90,000 which now the corporation loses.
The number of farmers in difficulty in this country today is the most disturbing figure since the 1930s. This is due to the devaluation of farm property. I have already described the case in northern Ontario.
The Farm Credit Corporation conducted a survey last summer. It was a sampling of 6,000 farm operations across the country and was properly carried out under Statistics Canada guidelines. It showed that some 39,000 farmers are in serious financial difficulty.
There are three criteria for classification of those in serious financial difficulty. First, a farmer's equity must be less than 15 per cent. Second, payment on the debt is more than 40 per cent of the gross. This means that a farmer with a $100,000 cash flow would fall under the criterion of being in serious financial difficulty if he was paying more than 40 per cent of that gross amount to meet the mortgage and interest payments. The third criterion is that the borrowings be greater than the capital investment. In other words, the farmer is borrowing to keep the farm in operation. A farmer would be in serious Financial difficulty if he met one of these three criteria.
While 39,000 farmers are in serious financial difficulty, the survey also showed that 1,700 of those surveyed had no equity left in their property. The fact that their debts were greater than their assets put them in a particularly difficult situation.

February 4, 1985
Farm Credit Act
The more remarkable aspect of this survey, as stated by the Chairman of the Board of the Farm Credit Corporation in the interview, is that the 39,000 or 17 per cent of farming operations in Canada in serious difficulty had risen to 45,000 or 20 per cent. The problem is becoming greater and the spinoff factors are also serious. I hope the Government will seriously consider my proposal that we provide the Farm Credit Corporation with the authority to give loan guarantees to individuals or corporate groups.

speechtext: Order, please. I recognize the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Blais).

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that we certainly appreciate the comments of the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). Perhaps it is regrettable that so few of his colleagues in the previous Government were here to pay close attention to his remarks, because we might not be in such a difficult economic situation as we are in now to come to grips with our agricultural problems, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member is suggesting that the Government ought to consider the advisability of amending the Farm Credit Act. In fact, he recommends that we provide for a guarantee to any person taking or holding a mortgage on farm property. I presume that there is no difference between the working proposed by the Hon. Member and his own thoughts, for I see in his representation an appeal to the Government to entertain the possibility of underwriting private mortgage loans rather than loans made by banks or other types of lending institutions, for if such is not the request of the Hon. Member, I can tell him right now that the Government is not prepared to consider that possibility.
However, Mr. Speaker, if his request is aimed at suggesting a new approach to promote greater participation by individuals in agricultural funding, I will say that our Government has already looked into that issue. Indeed, I think that the Hon. Member for Algoma is in a position to appreciate-he does not say so very often-the work and efforts of this Government to stabilize and improve the situation in the agricultural sector.
It is time members of various economic sectors in Canada regained control of their own destiny. Agriculture is one such sector. The Progressive Conservative Government's priority is to promote job creation and economic recovery. Agriculture is an important sector of our economy because many Canadians are directly engaged in it and even more work in a related field.
I would like to give a few figures which will help Hon. Members better understand the importance of agriculture in
the Canadian economy and, consequently, the priority given to this sector by our Government. In 1983, farm income amounted to $18.7 billion, which includes only the income earned in 1983, for a net agricultural income of over $3 billion. In that same year, all lending institutions granted farm loans totalling just under $10 billion. This includes banks, caisses populaires, trust companies, credit unions, mortgage loan companies, public financial institutions such as the Canada Farm Credit Corporation and its provincial counterparts, farm equipment dealers, cooperatives and, naturally, since this is what we are now discussing, private lenders.
Still in 1983, Mr. Speaker, banks provided $844 million in long-term credit to farmers. During the same period, the Canada Farm Credit Corporation granted $854 million in loans. In third place, private lenders provided approximately $376 million in loans. The average interest rate charged by the banks on these loans was 13.42 per cent, while the Farm Credit Corporation charged just under 13 per cent or 12.95 per cent. However, and this is worth mentioning, private lenders charged only 11.5 per cent.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, the interest rate on the $1.1 billion in long-term outstanding loans granted to private citizens in 1983 averaged 11.68 per cent, while commercial lenders charged more than 2 per cent more, namely 13.76 per cent on the $2.2 billion in outstanding loans.
Hon. Members will agree that the parties concerned can play a major role in agricultural financing. In this regard, we agree with the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). It is absolutely essential that we see to it that more individuals agree to finance the sale of their operation themselves. Such initiatives will help to restore confidence among Canadians, and our Government is determined to encourage this type of financing.
However, it must be kept in mind that, if interest rates which are generally lower than the market rates are to the advantage of the purchaser in this type of transaction, the process must also benefit the seller. If through some mechanism, the Government decided to provide a certain guarantee to private citizens who take mortgages on farm properties, three important results would ensue.
First, such an initiative would make this form of credit more attractive for farmers. It is easy to understand that a farmer who has worked all his life to build up his operation is not willing to sell it off. In addition, he is not necessarily willing to take over its financing. We should examine the fiscal consequences of such a transaction. With present provisions on capital gains, that procedure is not very profitable for farmers. To make such a measure efficient, the scope of the bill should be widened. This is the reason why the matter needs careful consideration.
A second consequence of such a guarantee would be felt in the level of capitalization of this particular industry. Agriculture is an industry where the income depends on many factors
February 4, 1985

on which producers have no control. Therefore, it is an industry where the return on capital is low and difficult to forecast on the short term. By encouraging retiring farmers to keep safe investment in the agricultural industry, for example, the capital accumulated through years of farming could be left in that sector.
A third consequence of such a program would be to provide individuals with an opportunity to invest directly in farming. The result would surely be a decreased demand of cash which the Government has to invest through its direct loans programs.
If I may, I would like to return to the costs of farm financing. I said a few minutes ago that interest rates set on transactions by individuals were usually lower than those of other lenders. A larger number of such transactions would increase the credit available at reasonable rates for farmers, especially young farmers. Some sort of guarantee offered by the Government could probably reduce the interest rates below the market level and would obviously reduce the costs of middlemen. Such a program could also greatly simplify the process of private financing.
I fully appreciate the motion moved by the Hon. Member, and I must emphasize that, as he can see, neither the Government nor I are against apple pie and motherhood. However, I should like to remind him of a number of issues which must be addressed before a federal guarantee program can be set up for privately financed transactions in the area of agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, there exist already some federal and provincial programs which guarantee in various ways the loans granted by commercial lenders. Naturally, these guarantees are given within the framework of programs with very specific objectives and vary from 10 per cent to 100 per cent of the total loans.
We are being asked to amend the Farm Credit Act, so that the Government may provide a guarantee to whoever is taking or holding a mortgage on a farm property. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member may be unaware that under certain circumstances, privately financed transactions are already covered by guarantees. For instance, a private mortgage which is followed by a second mortgage is essentially a first mortgage which is guaranteed by a second mortgage. The frequency of this phenomenon is poorly understood and requires a more in depth analysis.
Before deciding to set up such a program, it is necessary to properly identify the principles which would underline its operation. One of the conditions such a program should meet would be to make long term credit more affordable for farmers and especially new farmers who are beginning or want to expand.
We should also establish as a priority the conservation of capital in the farm industry. That should be a major consideration. This could be translated into long and short term fiscal benefits. Every precaution should be taken, however to prevent
Farm Credit Act
such a program from negatively affecting other areas of the economy. And private investments should not be made at the expense of other industries which are in such dire need of them.
As a matter of fact, if we had only this industry in which to work and correct past mistakes, it would be simpler, but there are several areas where the Government must intervene.
If ever the Government should implement a system of guarantees for privately financed mortgages, we should have to minimize the capitalization of benefits in the evaluation of assets. I can already hear the opposition blaming us for our material concerns, but we must face up to reality. There have been too many farm assistance programs which served only to put off the inevitable or, what is worse, which have hurt a whole generation of young farmers. We shall have to make sure that if the Government decides to provide mortgage guarantees, the prices of farms is not artificially inflated. Today, as Hon. Members are well aware, the price of land is dropping. Unfortunately, not only land values but also the value of many farmers' assets, paid for in years of hard work, is dropping as well. However, it would seem that when the price of land stabilizes, it will reach a level that is fairer and more equitable, considering the return on investment. What we would not need at this point is a Government that with a well-intentioned but poorly prepared program, becomes a major factor of inflation in the agricultural sector. Mr. Speaker, we can hardly be expected to introduce legislation that would reactivate the inflationary spiral we have been trying to control.
Those are the lines along which we would approach this question, and I would now like to explain some matters of a structural nature, Mr. Speaker.
I do not know whether the Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) is aware that a program similar to the one he is asking us to consider is in effect in New Zealand. I mention this particular country, Mr. Speaker, because its economy is very dependent on the performance of its agricultural industry, and as a result, on the New Zealand Government's agricultural policies. In New Zealand, tax exemptions, certain forms of guarantees and Treasury bonds have been used to encourage farmers to take the responsibility for financing the sale of their farm. Without necessarily intervening directly by guaranteeing mortgages, the Government helps the buyer take advantage of the vendor's terms. I have given this example, Mr. Speaker, to show Hon. Members that an effective program does not necessarily involve direct Government intervention. We know of course that the previous Government was extremely fond of this kind of direct intervention at every point in our daily lives. We must not continue along those lines, and it is our policy to get rid of this kind of intervention.
As far as Canada is concerned, Mr. Speaker, we must determine the total amount that could be guaranteed. What would be the ideal term for a given rate under such a pro-
1986

February 4, 1985
Farm Credit Act
gram? Ten years? More? Less? We would also have to calculate the level at which interest rates would have to be set. Should they be set according to the yield on Government of Canada bonds for comparable periods? Should they be set at a higher level? Could someone who already has a guaranteed loan borrow for a subsequent mortgage? How would a guarantee application be approved? There are many questions, Mr. Speaker.
And there are more. Since the Farm Credit Corporation is responsible for administering the Farm Credit Act, would it also be responsible for administering this program? Or should the program be administered by provincial agencies, by the vendor or by the buyer?
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House is not as straightforward as some Hon. Members would have us believe. I must say, however, that last November, at the agricultural financing conference, all provincial Ministers of Agriculture-the word "all" is important because there was a unanimity that we did not have before September 4 and that has been apparent in most of the meetings we have had with the provinces- recommended that this kind of guarantee be established. The federal-provincial task force on agricultural financing has also been considering this question.
One aspect I have not yet discussed but which must absolutely not be disregarded is that of the program funding, whether we like it or not. Clearly, this is not the Opposition's main concern. At least it has not been in the past. Whether we like it or not, this program will cost the Government something. But even before discussing any potential losses, we must look at how that kind of program would be funded.
I am quite aware that the costs would not be huge, but we must decide who will pay for them. Some will say that the Government should. But we, the Government Members, are not so sure of that. I can tell the House that, in view of our experience with other direct loan and guarantee programs, losses under such a program could reach 1 per cent of the principal lent out. Of course, during the first years, losses could be reduced to a minimum and their cost, if there was a need to recover the guarantee, would depend on the very structure of the program. The loss potential could be reduced to a minimum by only guaranteeing loans on real farm property. Losses could be controlled by a precise ratio of loans to guarantee, or still charges could simply be added to cover the losses. Those are various possibilities.
We cannot either get into loan guarantees without assessing what the demand would be for such a program. We know that in 1983, $376 million were loaned to individuals. How much guarantee should we provide to increase those transactions to the level required? The aim is not to launch a new program just for the sake of it. Success must be seen to be there, it must be obvious.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, some kind of bureaucracy would be needed to implement the program. Unfortunately, the previous Government created plenty of bureaucracy. We have no shortage of that! We must now work with what we have and try to maximize our returns. I think that the Farm Credit Corporation could play a role in this area, but its limits must be clearly defined.
I briefly referred to this earlier. A program of this kind would require amendments to the Income Tax Act. At the present time, farmers may defer capital gains over ten years if they sell the farm to a member of the family. The term is reduced to five if the farm is sold to someone outside the family. This will therefore have to be discussed with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, remind Hon. Members that this type of program would be of no help to farmers who are in financial difficulty. We will therefore have to consider and consult as well on new programs to help producers who really need assistance. All Members are concerned about this.
The Government is prepared to consider any realistic proposals to help Canadian farm producers. This is a priority, Mr. Speaker, and we have shown this quite clearly by certain concrete measures we have taken in the last three weeks, and I am sure no one will deny that. I am aware that the Hon. Member who proposed this amendment to the Farm Credit Act did so with the best of intentions. The proposal is an admirable one. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I would like to see this motion referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture. First, however, I would like to make the wording of the motion more precise. I move, Mr. Speaker, an amendment to the motion.

I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin):
That the motion be amended by striking out line 4 and substituting the following therefor:
"individual that takes or holds a mortgage on farm property."

Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to ask the Parliamentary Secretary a question about the use of the term

speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion, as amended, is one that I would strongly support. Most of us who have been in the House for a number of years have been addressing this type of problem of the general farm financial distress situation and farm financing difficulty almost ad nauseam. We have done so to the point where we have considered almost the whole range of things possible, broad sweeping changes to the Farm Credit Corporation and so on. We had an Opposition Day to consider a number of the measure that could be undertaken by the Government to help assist in resolving some of the financial difficulties in agriculture.
I take pleasure in being able to participate in this debate and debate to join in support of the motion to have the Standing Committee on Agriculture consider the motion as amended. This is one of the possible solutions to the difficulties that we face. It is one way that we might approach assisting agricultural financing.
Needless to say, if farm prices were high enough, we would not have a need to discuss this or a number of other measures in farm financing. The real world does not function that way. The prices that farmers and agricultural producers have been able to achieve have not been sufficient to provide adequate returns. We are left with the situation where there are a number of pressures and economic stresses that have to be addressed, unfortunately in piecemeal fashion sometimes.
Since World War II, Canadian agriculture has become a capital intensive industry that is subject to volatile world markerts. This suggests that farming businesses have become sensitive to various economic pressures, including variability of the cost of capital. However, we must be careful in our search for solutions not to look solely at isolated variables. It is the interaction of a number of economic factors which causes
Farm Credit Act
problems for the agricultural sector, and we must understand these if we are going to devise policies that are in harmony with the needs of the industry.
In the 1970s, farm real estate values were increasing faster than the rate of inflation. This had a strong impact on farmers entering the industry, on established farmers expanding their operations, on the transfer of land by retiring farmers, and on non-farmers who purchased farm land for investment purposes.
The net result of the farm investment decisions made in the 1970s about farm real estate is that the total level of farm debt has risen dramatically. Farmers borrowed money to buy or expand farms. Farm debt ballooned from $5 billion in 1972 to over $20 billion in 1982. The largest growth occurred in the long-term credit market because long-term credit tends to be used to purchase land. Long-term credit outstanding in Canada rose from $2.1 billion in 1982 to almost $10 billion in 1982.
In the seventies, land prices increased so rapidly that purchasing a farm, even at 100 per cent financing, seemed to be a good investment. In some years, the inflation of land prices provided a handsome return on investment even after paying interest costs. To give an example of how this worked, let us take a look at a peak year for land price inflation, that is, 1974. In that year, land prices inflated 27.7 per cent. Nominal interest rates were 7.3 per cent. This means that the real agricultural interest rate, which is the nominal rate minus land price inflation, amounted to minus 20 per cent. The impact of this is that farmers were in effect earning about 20 per cent on the money they borrowed to buy farm land.
These returns resulted in the demand for credit to expand. Commercial lending institutions began moving to the farm mortgage market. Producers bought land, acquired modern buildings and purchased new equipment, betting that land prices would keep on going up. In the 1980s the bubble burst.
Today, land prices have dropped. Interest charges are higher than in the 1970s. The real agricultural interest rate in 1984 was over 20 per cent, which meant that farmers' investments were eroding. Consequently, the demand for credit has sharply declined. To give an example, as of January 15, the Farm Credit Corporation has committed only about $200 million. This compares to about $700 million for the same period the year before.
The consecutive declines in cash flows and purchasing power have forced many farmers to reduce their debt by offering some or all of their land for sale, but there have been few buyers. This has reduced or stagnated land prices. Those who could wait no longer to sell were forced to leave farming, producing a record number of bankruptcies. We know that some commodity groups, such as beef and hog producers, have been harder hit than others.
The trends that I have described show the general economic framework affecting farmers. Not all farmers are in difficulty. A Farm Credit Corporation survey carried out earlier this year indicates which farmers are experiencing problems.

February 4, 1985
Farm Credit Act
The survey shows that the over-all equity position of farmers has declined. In the first farm survey in 1981, farmers owned on average 85 per cent of the assets of their farms. Three years later, their equity had declined to 82 per cent. This is still a strong equity position. However, the industry averages do not tell the full story.
The equity positions of farmers in each region were, as analysed by dividing farmers, in three equal groups according to the amount of equity they hold-low, medium or high equity. While the numbers change from region to region, the average equity of the low-equity group is far below that of the remaining two-thirds of farmers.
In Alberta, for example, the top equity group has an equity position that approaches 100 per cent. The middle group's equity average is 91 per cent. The bottom group's average equity is only 62 per cent. Across Canada, the low-equity group, or one-third of farmers, holds over three-quarters of the farm debt. If production were distributed equally, that would not be a serious problem.
The significance of this finding is that the farmers holding most of the debt tend to be the nation's youngest and most productive farmers. It is not a question of the debt being concentrated in an unimportant sector of agriculture. It is a question of the debt being concentrated in the mainstream of commercial farming. About half of the farm product sales come from this low-equity group.
The farmers across Canada who are experiencing severe and moderate stress are not necessarily headed for bankruptcy. It is estimated that some 1,700 of the farmers in the severe stress category may be on the verge of insolvency because their debts exceed their assets. This means that out of a national total of over 228,000 farms, less than 1 per cent of farmers are in immediate danger of financial collapse. However, the farmers in the severe and moderate stress categories are probably experiencing cash flow problems. They may be falling behind in the payments on their debts.
As of January 1, 1985, about 16,500 or 21 per cent of FCC's 79,000 loan accounts were in arrears for a total of about $197 million. I believe there are two broad considerations when looking at policy to meet the financing needs of Canadian farmers. The first is that we must devise programs so that we can help farmers in difficulty. The second is to consider policies that will meet the long-term needs of the industry.
I want to spend a moment talking very specifically about one thing. Before doing so, I would mention the support that has been given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to agriculture and our agricultural producers in the last three or four months. The Minister of Finance started in his November 8 statement by helping to reduce input costs by relieving some of the tax burden on farm fuels. That was one thing. The second thing he has done, and followed up in the last week with a background paper, is to indicate that there will be a House of Commons standing committee or subcommittee to consider capital gains, agri-bonds and Section 31 aspects of agricultural financing.
Doesn't sound very hopeful.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
It is with the hope that they will at least produce an interim report prior to the budget that will be brought down in the spring. Those are solid things that the Minister of Finance has done specifically and all together. I think they represent probably three or four times the level of support in three months that we had in the last four or five years from the Ministers of Finance of the previous Government.
The Minister of Agriculture has also made his mark in a very short time by reducing interest rates of the Farm Credit Corporation. All of those interest rates were above 14 per cent and some of them were as high as 16.75 per cent. Those rates are now down to 12.75 per cent, and this represents a real contribution toward reducing some of the pressures on the agricultural borrower.
As mentioned by the Parliamentary Secretary, we hope that the stabilization Bill will be before the Standing Committee in the very near future. As well, the federal-provincial Ministers' conference that has been held to look at agricultural lending is another important step in looking at the broad perspective. In a very short time, I would suggest, we have made our mark on trying to work out some of the problems that have gradually built up over the last number of years.
One of the final points about which I will spend a moment or two speaking is the effort to assist the people who are in difficulty now and who have problems that they may not be able to resolve no matter how well we can get some of these changes like the changes to the Farm Credit Corporation on track. The Minister of Agriculture indicated that there would be a moratorium on farm credit bankruptcies, and that was in place until January 15 of this year. As that moratorium was lifted, the Minister indicated that there would be an appeal board process through an expanded appeal board of the Farm Credit Corporation across the country. That process is now in place and is looking at those cases of the Farm Credit Corporation which could not see viability.
At the same time, the Minister lent his support to a pilot project in the Counties of Bruce and Grey, which will end on March 21 of this year. This project saw an extraordinary level of co-operation from the local agricultural community, the Canadian Bankers Association, the Farm Credit Corporation and the provincial Ministry. This seven-person board is now meeting, hearing cases and making proposals, some of which have very creative aspects, and these proposals will then be returned to the Farm Credit Corporation and other lenders for their consideration. The process itself is working very well. It has the respect and co-operation of all those involved to this point in time.
I think the final determination of whether or not this or other processes will be useful will have to wait until they are finished and we see the reaction and response of the lending institutions. However, in the end, I think it will be another example of how the Government is actually attempting to solve
February 4, 1985

some of the problems that have been allowed to exist over a long period of time. I lend my support to the Hon. Member's motion as another example of things to which we can look in an effort to create additional support in the agricultural lending field.
Mr. Speaker, I am a bit concerned that you did not recognize me as third speaker as that is a tradition of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. Perhaps that is something the Hon. Member might be able to take up with the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and his parliamentary committee. Perhaps Private Members' Hour should be extended to two hours. The Chair cannot recognize everyone in the House during a one hour period.

Mr. Speaker, this approach to farm credit is not unique and it is not new. It has been suggested on many occasions, and the previous Government had the opportunity to put it into place. It sounds very good. Perhaps it is even very practical. However, I could say many things about it that would make it seem unacceptable.
I thank the Hon. Member from the Government side who gave us a very technical approach to the possibilities for and against the motion as it stands. However, what we really need to discuss here is not farm credit but the situation in which agriculture finds itself. We are now in a position in which farm credit is only one of the very small issues for which we have some concern. In fact, this particular motion which might change a small part of the Farm Credit Corporation Act is a band-aid upon a band-aid. It is suggesting that we will help farmers who are in trouble to get more money by providing guarantees to the lender. The banks can tell us right now that there is no shortage of money to lend. The guarantee is necessary, and for that reason I will support the motion put by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster).
In many ways, this band-aid is not a very effectual one because credit is only one of the problems facing agriculture. If it were possible for farmers to face the need for credit, then we would be talking about something that would be worthwhile. We would be having a worth-while debate. As the previous speaker suggested, perhaps all we need to do is to put into effect some kind of a guaranteed price for the products of the farmers. Then we would not have to worry about all these little band-aids which will take care of credit or the cost of farm fuel or things like that. We need to have a global debate on the problems of the farm and look at those problems all together rather than look at each small problem as it comes up.
Over the years, the input cost of farmers have increased by about 300 per cent. In the same period of time of eight or ten years, the commody price has not increased perceivably. We have a situation in which incomes are going down or staying the same and the costs are rising. There are many other solutions at which we could be looking. We should be looking at them now and we should be looking at them all together.
Adjournment Debate
This Government and apparently the previous Government were afraid to look at parity as a possibility which would help farmers. They were unable to suggest reducing the price of credit entirely so that it would not become a factor in the elimination of farmers from the business.
We need to be debating a straightforward income security program for farmers which would make these kinds of band-aids unnecessary. Then we would be going in a direction which would allow farmers to know that if they produce well, they will survive and make a good living for themselves and their families. If we can have that kind of government-sponsored global approach to agriculture, it would be worth-while. These band-aids are not worth bringing before the House.

speechtext:

That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending the Farm Credit Act in order to provide for a guarantee to any individual that takes or holds a mortgage on farm property.
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion as submitted?

Agreed.
Motion (Mr. Foster) as amended agreed to.
