subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS- CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES. (B) REVIEWS OF EQUALIZATION PAYMENT MADE TO MANITOBA
FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS- CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES. (B) REVIEWS OF EQUALIZATION PAYMENT MADE TO MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I want to use the opportunity that this adjournment debate offers to bring to the attention of the House the very serious economic position which the Province of Manitoba faces and the need for immediate action by the federal Government both to come to grips with the serious problem of equalization payments and to fulfil the commitments which were made by the previous Government to provide information and a review of the equalization formula, which is essential for the provision of jobs and economic growth.
On November 27 I raised a question with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had gone through his somewhat unusual technique of releasing information by dropping it in a hotel lobby. At that

February 4, 1985
Adjournment Debate
time, I asked whether the instructions which were given by the Deputy Minister of Finance-which was to keep Manitobans loose and easy, but that no commitments were to be given- was in fact the position of the Government. Of course, we did not receive an answer to that question.
What concerns me most is that when the original formula for equalization came forward, the previous Government agreed to a transition period in which the payments would go from $400 million a year to $480 million a year. The previous administration recognized that there would be a transition period which would provide a cushioning effect during the time that the new formula was being put into place.
We all know the reason for the new formula. It was implemented during the time of the economic downturn, when the formula went from a ten province average to a five province average. If that had not been done, some of the richest provinces in the country would have been able to cut into equalization payments. There was a very clear rationale for it. An adjustment was required and the previous administration provided a three-year adjustment period. However, by 1983 it was clear that because of the economic repercussions of the recession, the formula which was originally devised in 1982 and the forecasts which were based on that formula would not be fulfilled. At that point in time our Government agreed that it was important to review the formula and the equalization agreements and to share that information with the Province of Manitoba in order to renegotiate a settlement. On behalf of the Government of the day, I communicated that information to the Manitoba Government in July of 1984.
The important question is: Has that review been undertaken, and if so, why has the new Government not been prepared to bring forward the results of the review and share those results with the Government and the people of Manitoba? It is quite clear that conditions have changed. We recognized the changing conditions and therefore we recognized the need to renegotiate the settlement. If that is not done, the Province of Manitoba is likely to suffer a loss of approximately $72 million in its new fiscal year, which begins in March. It will have a very severe impact on education, social services and the provisions of a wide variety of activities in the Province of Manitoba. It is important for the Government to come clean and put on the public record-and certainly with the Government of Manitoba-what it discovered in the review that the financial officials were asked to undertake and, as well, to renegotiate a new settlement.
At the same time as there has been a reluctance to deal with the equalization payment issue, we have also experienced an enormous number of severe cut-backs in the Province of Manitoba. For example, the cut-backs in the National Research Council laboratories, the substantial reduction in grants under the IRDP, and the recent cancellation of the VIA Rail centre. The estimate, as a result of those cuts, is that over
4,000	permanent jobs will be lost and 2,000 jobs will not be there for summer students. Manitoba has perhaps suffered more than any other province because of government cutbacks, and at the same time the situation is being compounded by the lack of response to the equalization problem.
The Minister of Finance of the Government of Manitoba and a number of people from social services and educational institutions in Manitoba visited Ottawa last week. They simply asked for a willingness to come to grips with it. It is our hope that the Government will now respond and recognize that it has inflicted major economic damage on the province through its cut-backs and it should not further enhance and aggravate that damage by not coming to grips with the equalization problem. There was a commitment made by the last Government to come to grips with the program, to negotiate it, review it and reach a new settlement. I believe it is incumbent upon the Conservative Government to live up to the kinds of commitments which were made last year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Gustafson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS- CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES. (B) REVIEWS OF EQUALIZATION PAYMENT MADE TO MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to respond to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) on the subject of Manitoba's equalization entitlements. As he well knows, the principle of the equalization program and the important role it plays in ensuring that all provincial Governments have sufficient revenues to provide an appropriate level of services to their populations, have never been a matter of debate among the three Parties represented in this House. This is reflected in the fact that those principles are now enshrined in the Constitution Act, 1982. However, the Hon. Member expressed concern that this Government is not consulting with Manitoba in reviewing a specific part of this program, the transitional guarantee which the previous Government, of which he was a member, was responsible for introducing.
The Hon. Member seems unaware that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has been consulting continually with all of his provincial counterparts, most recently with all provincial Finance Ministers on January 15 in Montreal. This was the reason he met with the Manitoba Minister in Winnipeg on November 26. The Minister of Finance had a very productive meeting with Mr. Schroeder, and the issue of the transitional equalization payments was discussed in a frank and cordial manner. The Hon. Member will know, too, that the two Ministers met again last week.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry also asked whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was aware of the previous Government's commitment to review the transitional guarantee and to share information from this review with the provinces. The Minister of Finance is indeed reviewing this matter and, as I noted, has been consulting with Manitoba and other provinces. The issue of the transitional guarantee is indeed an important one, both for Manitoba and for Quebec, which is also affected. The Minister of Finance is currently examining this matter in the over-all context of the fiscal situation we inherited and how our policies will affect all provinces.
February 4, 1985

Our policy of ongoing consultations and openness with the provinces since September 17 on these and other matters Mr. Speaker, is a good one. I might add, it is a policy which was not pursued by the previous Government. These consultations with the Provinces have continued and will continue. The transitional payment in question will be fully reviewed and the Government will soon be in a position to come to some conclusions on Manitoba's stated concerns.

subtopic: NUCLEAR ENERGY-REQUEST FOR PARLIAMENTARY INQUIRY INTO INDUSTRY. (B) INDUSTRY'S ACCOUNTABILITY
NUCLEAR ENERGY-REQUEST FOR PARLIAMENTARY INQUIRY INTO INDUSTRY. (B) INDUSTRY'S ACCOUNTABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to follow up on a question I asked of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) on November 20. At that time I asked if the Government was going to be true to the intentions of the Progressive Conservative Government in 1979 and initiate a parliamentary inquiry into all aspects of the nuclear industry in Canada. The Minister's answers to me at that time were very disturbing in so far as she indicated that she would be consulting only with officials of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the nuclear industry in Ontario and New Brunswick as to whether or not such an inquiry was a good idea.
What kind of advice does the Minister expect the AECL and the nuclear industry? Does she expect them to invite public scrutiny by telling her to go ahead with an inquiry? Why did she not also make a commitment to discuss the usefulness of such an inquiry with the Canadian Coalition for Nuclear Responsibility, for example, or others who take a more critical and less self-serving view of the nuclear option?
It is over two months now since I asked the question of the Minister and she has said nothing about an inquiry. If you look at her answer of November 20, you see that the writing was on the wall. She said to me that, "The problems may perhaps lie more in the marketing area", a statement which reveals very clearly the uncritical attitude she takes toward the nuclear power question. The kind of inquiry I have in mind would be one that goes deeper than she is obviously prepared to go and asks whether things like nuclear reactors are what we ought to be marketing at all, even if we could successfully market them, which we have not been able to do to date.
Tragically, the Minister seems to be able to reflect on the nuclear power question only from a commercial point of view rather than from an ethical or environmental point of view. This kind of myopia on the Minister's part is very frightening.
Take, for example, her view of the concern expressed by many Manitobans over Atomic Energy of Canada's underground research laboratory at Lac du Bonnet. In answer to a July 20, 1984 letter from the town council of Gimli, she responds to their resolution of concern about the disposal of radioactive waste by saying with respect to the disposal of radioactive waste from other countries that "such a project could offer considerable commercial benefits". This statement, taken together with the fact that the Americans are now
Adjournment Debate
considering making an investment in the underground research laboratory at Lac du Bonnet, is hardly reassuring to those of us who want to stop and reflect on the nuclear option as a whole and who want assurances that under no circumstances whatsoever will Manitoba become a radioactive garbage dump for the rest of Canada, the United States, or the world.
I call on the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to answer the letter he received from the Committee of Concerned Citizens of Manitoba, and to meet their request that he publicly instruct AECL that, as a matter of policy, Manitoba is not and will not be a location for radioactive garbage dump. I also call again on the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to initiate a full parliamentary inquiry into the nuclear industry as recently asked for by the British Columbia Medical Association who, like myself, has been pressing for such an inquiry for several years.
In introduced a Private Member's Bill to this effect in 1980 and I intend to do so again in this Parliament as I try, in any way I can as a Member of Parliament, to stimulate the debate which is so necessary on this issue. The fact that so far the Government has been able to get away with business as usual on the nuclear side, and massive cuts in the renewable energy research, environmental monitoring, and wildlife conservation, does not bode well for the future. I invite those who share my concerns to let me know so that we can work together to change the mind of the Government.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NUCLEAR ENERGY-REQUEST FOR PARLIAMENTARY INQUIRY INTO INDUSTRY. (B) INDUSTRY'S ACCOUNTABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) for the question and the follow-up which allows us to discuss this tonight.
Over the past decade the various aspects of Canada's nuclear fuel cycle have been the subject of a number of comprehensive federal and provincial inquiries and reviews. Two major inquiries were undertaken in Ontario, the producer of 85 per cent of the country's nuclear generated electricity. The Ontario Royal Commission on Electric Power Planning, commonly known as the Porter Commission, devoted a considerable amount of time to scrutinizing Ontario's nuclear power program, as did the Ontario Select Committee on Hydro Affairs. As of the present time we are awaiting the report from the interfaith hearings on nuclear energy sponsored by a number of groups including the Anglican diocese, the Jewish community, the Roman Catholic archdiocese, the United Church and the Baha'i community.
In Saskatchewan, the Cluff Lake Board of Inquiry-the Bayda Commission-examined the expansion of uranium mining in that province. While like the two Ontario inquiries, the Bayda Commission studies all aspects of the nuclear fuel cycle from uranium mining to radioactive waste to disposal, it also examined nuclear ethics highlighting the nuclear proliferation issue. It is encouraging to note that all three inquiries supported the continuation of Canada's nuclear programs.
In addition to these large scale inquiries a number of smaller, more specific inquiries have been conducted. Federal-

February 4, 1985
Adjournment Debate
ly, an environmental assessment review panel reported on four different locations for a new uranium refinery in Ontario. A panel report was also presented on a proposed uranium refinery site in Saskatchewan. Provincial inquiries relating to uranium mining have been conducted in Newfoundland and Labrador and in British Columbia.
A federal study entitled the Nuclear Industry Review was released by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in the summer of 1982. The report concluded that long-term prospects for the domestic nuclear industry are favourable as nuclear power is the most economical choice for new electricity generation in many parts of our country today. Despite the current downturn in demand, CANDU remains an attractive generating technology both for domestic and some export markets. While this report recognized that Government initiatives might be required to preserve manufacturing in the short term until domestic demand is sufficient to sustain it, the immediate positive economic spinoff of such initiatives cannot be discounted.
As the federal Government enters a new era, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has indicated her interest in investigating the usefulness of such an inquiry as was suggested by the Hon. Member. The Minister has stated that such an inquiry could consider, among other things, what role the industry might play within the energy sector, the international marketing of CANDU reactors, which the Hon. Member seems to criticize, the electricity exports to the United States and the production of heavy water.
The Minister reiterated just two weeks ago her commitment to review nuclear matters. The Hon. Member says she has not mentioned it in two months. She mentioned it just two weeks ago when commenting on the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada's report Connections: An Energy Strategy for the Future. At that time she promised to study closely the Council's recommendations dealing with nuclear energy, particularly those relating to continued government support of Canada's nuclear technology. I can assure the Member that this investigation is going on and we will be reporting the findings to the House in the not too distant future.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-STUDENT SUMMER JOBS. (B) ALLOCATION OF FUNDS. (C) GOVERNMENT CONSULTATION
EMPLOYMENT-STUDENT SUMMER JOBS. (B) ALLOCATION OF FUNDS. (C) GOVERNMENT CONSULTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 28, I directed a question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss Macdonald) about a document which describes a program called SELF, which stands for Summer Experience and Learning Fund.
I asked the Minister if it was not true that the document described expenditures amounting to $140 million which would provide summer employment for some 65,000 students. On that occasion the Minister indicated that a program would be announced after she has had an opportunity to consult with
all those sectors of the community that were worthy of consultation.
In response, I pointed out that the Canadian Federation of Students were told, in response to a request for a meeting, that essentially the Minister would not be able to meet with the Canadian Federation of Students in the foreseeable future.
On the subsequent day the Minister discovered that indeed, as the document indicates, she had seen and agreed to a program called SELF which is described in intimate detail, with the implication that it will be the basis for the implementation of a summer student employment program after approval by Cabinet. Furthermore, I determined on that same day that in spite of the previous denial of an opportunity for the Canadian Federation of Students to meet with her, she had indeed agreed to meet with them.
There has been some change in direction. I hope that this change in direction will continue and that these consultations with the Canadian Federation of Students and others will bring about a modification to some elements of the program that I think are subject to criticism and concern.
I should point out that the program's very title indicates a considerable shift in emphasis from a job-creation program to a training program. In fact, what has been done is to use Summer Career Access as the basis for a $108 million program. There are difficulties with that because I think most of us realize that not every job available will be appropriate to the particular kind of vocational training or education that a student is pursuing in a college or university. There will be some problem of fit. I do not want to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is a basic objection to the appropriateness, indeed the value, of having summer jobs which are matched to the degree or diploma a student is pursuing. The difficulty is that the entire program will be of that character, and I think this suggests considerable difficulties.
One of the major difficulties is that last year the deadline for applications for Summer Canada projects was February 24, with an announcement made in December. I think that should make it clear to you, Sir, that we are already very late in the year in advancing a program that will be accessible and useful to students. I think it is not going too far to suggest that students must feel some considerable insecurity and doubt about the availability of jobs.
First, let us focus on the fact that the Minister has reiterated the point, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), in describing the cuts applicable to Summer Canada, said that $85 million was involved and 40,000 student jobs. Although $85 million was budgeted, $201.9 million was spent creating
86,000	jobs. Will the Minister consider advancing a program that will at least ensure that the same number of student job placements will be created in 1985 as were created in 1984?
Will it not be reasonable, in view of the lateness of the hour, to consider reducing the career access portion, that is ICE and centers for the career employment portion to the level of the pilot programs or at least to introduce more flexibility in the
February 4, 1985

program to counter the eventuality that there will not be enough career places to satisfy the needs for student employment?
There are a number of other aspects of this program that I think are subject to considerable concern. There is the concern, first, that Summer Canada was previously a project-oriented program that served the community needs of a number of people in this country who suffered one difficulty or another. I am speaking of the disabled, women, the unemployed and so on who were served in many communities by student groups. There is a great deal of concern about that. It would be very desirable from the point of view of this vast number of community organizations helping the deprived and the dispossessed, if that portion of the program were again introduced, that is to say, that the project-oriented portion be given increased emphasis compared to what is suggested in the document, and that the community benefit aspect of Summer Canada be considered again as appropriate.
I should point out that in the past there was an affirmative action aspect to the program requiring that places be reserved for the disabled, women, natives and so on. We would like to see that reinstated.
There is another element in the program that concerns me also. There is a portion of the program which is based on a United Way type of campaign which depends upon private business to create jobs by a kind of propaganda effort. What worries me is that it is recommended in the document, and I hope this will be turned down, that moneys will be withdrawn from ICE, that is a wage subsidy program, in order to encourage the successful implementation of the voluntary program. I think that speaks of considerable dangers to student employment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-STUDENT SUMMER JOBS. (B) ALLOCATION OF FUNDS. (C) GOVERNMENT CONSULTATION
speechtext:
On behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer the question of my colleague from Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy).
I must admit that I am a little bit surprised that the Hon. Member should raise his question this evening because, if we
Adjournment Debate
look at Hansard, it first came up last Monday. The question was raised in the House by my colleague on January 28, and the Minister did say that programs would be announced within about two weeks. Still, I am glad that my colleague has mentioned the fact that the consultation and the points raised last week have led to some results. Mr. Speaker, it goes to show that the Minister of Employment and Immigration is open to all suggestions, be it to meet with students or to answer a question on a document which has now been put into circulation and which, at the request of the Hon. Member, is the subject of a special study.
Very soon, the Minister of Employment and Immigration will announce new programs. As you know, she is now consulting the provinces, the Northwest Territories, companies, workers, students and young Canadians.
As to the questions raised by my colleague, namely: Will the same number of jobs be guaranteed? Can existing programs be replaced by other programs so as to save the same number of jobs, community projects and positive action projects, I should think that the Minister will consider the question, that it is the subject of current consultations, and that it will be included in the announcement which the Minister said last Monday would be made within about two weeks.
The Government is perfectly aware of the situation of young people, that what they need most is good job opportunities. They do not want to walk down a dead-end street as they did before. Mr. Speaker, that is why I think a distinction has to be made between being late in the year and being late, period. I know that this year the summer programs will be announced later than last year, but that does not mean we are too late. Hon. Members of the Opposition have been raising a fuss because the programs have not yet been announced, but I rest assured that all Canadian youths are patiently waiting for those new programs and, as the Minister told me, I can assure you that the announcement is forthcoming and that nobody will be disappointed.
